The Philippines is facing concerns over two alleged government data leaks involving the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR).

However, neither agency has verified the amount of information allegedly stolen or whether the records advertised online were genuine.

In a press release dated the 9th of November, the SEC detected the security incident that happened on the 6th of November and concluded that the personal information linked to individual accounts may have been exposed.

This includes names, usernames, contact details, dates of birth, residential addresses, and taxpayer identification numbers. However, the agency further clarified that its company records, internal databases, and passwords remained unaffected.

Additional technical safeguards and monitoring rules across the Commission’s digital infrastructure have likewise been implemented to prevent potential vulnerabilities and recurrence.

For now, the SEC added technical safeguards and monitoring rules to prevent recurrence. Meanwhile, the public is advised to follow six precautionary steps to stay vigilant this time. This includes,

At the same time, the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) is separately investigating claims that approximately 340,000 lines of taxpayer information were being offered for sale online. The SEC faced a similar allegation involving 487,000 lines of information.

However, these figures represent advertised records, not confirmed victims. Since both claims originated from the same account, neither independently validates the other.

This coincided with the Brazilian crypto exchange Mercado Bitcoin suspending deposits and withdrawals on the 2nd of November after detecting a security incident in one of its systems. This further followed a series of crypto security concerns, including Binance’s reported $6.3 billion exploit.

#5176. HIVE Reports $84.9M Revenue as AI GPU Business Grows 71% Amid Mining Pressures

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

TL;DR: HIVE Digital reported $84.9 million in fiscal second-quarter revenue and roughly 71% growth in its AI-focused BUZZ GPU business. The company also recorded a substantial quarterly loss, including a mining-equipment impairment. The results show both the promise and cost of shifting computing capacity toward AI services.

Bitcoin miners have spent much of 2026 trying to turn their access to electricity, land and data centers into businesses that can serve more than one market. HIVE Digital’s latest numbers put a price tag on that strategy.

The company said its fiscal second quarter, ended September 30, 2026, brought in approximately $84.9 million of revenue. Its BUZZ high-performance-computing division generated about $8.8 million, an increase of 70.7% from the comparable period. HIVE also reported about $139 million in cash on the balance sheet.

The growth is meaningful, but the AI arm remains far smaller than the company’s combined operations. A rapidly growing new division does not automatically replace the economics of Bitcoin mining.

HIVE reported a quarterly net loss in the region of $78 million and included a mining-equipment impairment of approximately $31.2 million. Impairments are generally noncash accounting charges in the period they are recorded, but they can still indicate that expected future economic value has fallen.

That distinction is important. A loss containing a major impairment is not the same as the business spending an identical amount of cash in the quarter. Equally, treating impairments as irrelevant would miss what they say about the pressure on older machines or assumptions about their earning potential.

Mining hardware has a useful life shaped by electricity prices, network difficulty, equipment efficiency and Bitcoin’s market value. When those assumptions change, a fleet that looked attractive two years ago may not justify its former carrying value.

The case for AI data centers is that demand for specialized computing may offer a revenue stream less closely tied to Bitcoin’s mining difficulty. But supplying GPU services requires capital, customer relationships, network infrastructure and operational expertise different from the work of running application-specific mining rigs.

NewsBTC has tracked miners making that transition, including Riot’s Bitcoin sales alongside its AI-data-center ambitions. HIVE’s BUZZ expansion is another version of the same strategic question: how quickly can an established miner earn durable income from compute services?

Partnerships and infrastructure projects are relevant here too. Our reporting on TeraWulf’s growth in AI leasing shows how the business of securing power-intensive sites and monetizing them through leases has become competitive. Possessing a data center does not guarantee demand for the GPUs housed in it.

Future reports should clarify how much revenue the AI division earns, whether its margins justify continued capital investment and how the mining segment performs as difficulty changes. Total company revenue can rise or fall for reasons unrelated to the profitability of the new computing business.

Investors should also watch the company’s liquidity, debt commitments and equipment spending. The $139 million cash figure is helpful context, but not a substitute for understanding cash consumption and future construction obligations.

HIVE is presenting itself as a dual-engine business. The latest quarter demonstrates that GPU services are growing quickly, while the bottom-line loss shows why the transition remains a work in progress rather than an accomplished turnaround.

#5175. ADA, XRP, DOGE: Gemini Names Biggest Losers of 2026

Crypto exchange Gemini has unveiled the biggest losers in the altcoin space for 2026 so far, as many of the crypto world's biggest digital currencies have been seeing massive double-digit price plunges.

Crypto exchange Gemini recently shared a list of 10 cryptocurrencies that have seen particularly brutal losses since the start of 2026 in a post on the X social media platform.

Topping Gemini's list of the biggest losers for this year is Bitcoin Cash (BCH), which has crashed a shocking 61.76% year-to-date.

Coming in second is Polkadot (DOT), with a 53.03% price decline, while Cardano (ADA) holds third place after shedding 48.04% of its value.

Ripple-related XRP and the top meme cryptocurrency Dogecoin (DOGE) are next in line, with losses of 43.43% and 42.38%, respectively.

Several other major cryptocurrencies are also seeing considerable losses, such as Sui (SUI), which has fallen 42.08%, Hedera (HBAR), which has dropped 38.13%, Solana (SOL), down 34.02%, Avalanche (AVAX), which has lost 33.40%, and Kaspa (KAS), which has gone down 30.75%.

Declining liquidity in the market, weakening speculative interest, lackluster institutional interest and general macroeconomic conditions are all major factors causing most major altcoins to underperform so far.

But for some, other issues within their ecosystems are also proving troublesome.

For instance, in the case of Cardano, the platform is seeing limited decentralized finance activity. As of Nov. 9, the total value locked in its DeFi ecosystem reportedly dropped below $50 million.

While Ripple continues its expansion in the institutional payments sector, stablecoin and tokenization areas, this hasn't necessarily led to sustained buying interest in XRP.

In fact, spot trading volume for XRP fell 53.5%, while perpetual futures trading volume dropped 44%.

Dogecoin, on the other hand, has been contending with waning speculative interest in meme cryptocurrencies.

Its institutional investment narrative also hasn't really caught on yet, with Bitwise announcing in September the shutdown of its Dogecoin ETF as the product failed to draw investor interest.

Bitcoin Cash has been seeing particularly sharp declines as it is now experiencing a reversal of its stellar 2025 performance, when the cryptocurrency soared around 38%.

Selling pressure picked up in May and June 2026 as BCH saw back-to-back monthly drops of over 30%.

A rebound could be seen in September after CME Group announced Bitcoin Cash futures, but this proved insufficient to stop the ongoing downtrend.

#5174. Top 12 Crypto Debit Cards to Consider

Home » Cryptopedia » Top 12 Crypto Debit Cards to Consider

Compare fees, cashback, availability, and features of 12 crypto cards to find the right option for your spending needs.

Crypto debit cards are no longer just a way to convert Bitcoin into cash for everyday purchases. In 2026, there are plenty of options, from exchange-linked cards and stablecoin payment solutions to self-custody cards connected directly to crypto wallets.

But choosing one isn’t just about cashback. Availability depends on your country, better rewards may require staking or a paid subscription, and fees can quickly eat into your benefits. It’s also worth checking how each card works, as some are prepaid debit cards while others offer credit backed by crypto holdings.

We’ve selected 12 crypto cards worth considering in 2026, comparing their features, fees, rewards, and availability to help you find the right option, whether you prioritize low fees, stablecoin spending, cashback, or control over your assets.

The Coinbase Card Visa prepaid debit card that lets US customers (excluding Hawaii) spend directly from their Coinbase accounts.

It is a custodial card, meaning funds remain in your Coinbase account and are deducted when you make a purchase. Coinbase automatically converts crypto to USD at checkout or for ATM withdrawals, so merchants never receive crypto. You also get a virtual card as soon as you’re approved, with Apple Pay and Google Pay support.

Fees are relatively low. There are no annual fees or charges for spending USD or crypto, including USDC. Coinbase Card does not charge monthly or foreign transaction fees, and there are no Coinbase ATM withdrawal fees (though ATM operators may charge their own). The main cost is Coinbase’s crypto conversion spread. Spending USD or USDC avoids it, making them the cheapest funding options.

Crypto rewards are the main attraction, but rates vary. Rewards are optional, available to US users, and paid in a crypto asset of your choice from a rotating list. Rates are displayed in the app, can be changed at any time, and have no stated cap. Although many reviews advertise rates of up to 4%, Coinbase does not guarantee a fixed rate on its official card page. Check the current in-app offer before applying.

Best for: US-based Coinbase users who want a simple, low-fee card and crypto rewards without a credit check.

Crypto.com’s crypto debit card depends on your region. In the US, it is now a Visa Signature credit card issued by Comenity Capital Bank through Bread Financial. Cardholders can earn rewards in BTC or CRO, but approval requires a credit check. Applications are made through the Crypto.com app.

Rewards range from roughly 1.5% to 5–6%, depending on the tier. However, higher Level Up tiers require locking up or staking CRO. Those who don’t want to commit CRO can choose the entry tier.

Outside the US, the card remains a prepaid debit card. In the European Economic Area (EEA), the free tier offers no cashback, while the Plus plan (€4.99/month) starts at 2% cashback.

Best for: Users who already hold CRO and want to maximize rewards.

KAST is a Visa debit card that that spends a USD balance funded with stablecoins. It offers three tiers: Standard (free, 1.5% cashback), Premium ($1000 a year, 2% cashback) and Private ($10,000 a year, 3%).

Cashback is paid in dollars, rather than tokens. Monthly cashback limits apply: $2,000 in spend for Standard, $10,000 for Premium and $40,000 for Private.

However, KAST fees can reduce the returns. Foreign exchange fees on KAS crypto debit card range from 0.5% to 1.75%, while a physical Standard card costs $40 to deliver.

KAST estimates Standard users may keep up to 1% cashback after FX fees. Premium and Private also include a Visa Infinite card and KAST Points on eligible spending.

Best for: Fequent stablecoin spenders, especially those spending in USD.

Krak, Kraken’s money app, launched its Visa debit card in the US in August 2026. Available as a physical and virtual card, it lets users spend from 600+ fiat and crypto assets, with purchases converted to USD at checkout. The card is issued by Lead Bank and powered by Stripe Issuing.

Krak offers up to 2% cashback in USD or Bitcoin, paid after transactions settle, with no monthly or annual fees.

Rewards depend on users’ average asset balances across Krak, Kraken and Kraken Pro. The card is available in all US states except New York, Maine, Massachusetts and Indiana. Crypto-funded purchases may incur conversion spreads and trigger taxable events.

Best for: US users who hold a mix of crypto and cash and want one card for everything.

The MetaMask Card lets users spend directly from their self-custody wallet, without preloading funds. Built with Mastercard and Baanx (now Monavate) and issued by Cross River Bank in the US, it works wherever Mastercard is accepted, including online, in-store and through Apple Pay or Google Pay. Unlike exchange cards, MetaMask Card allows to retain full control of your crypto until purchase.

The card has two tiers: the standard card offers 1% cashback in mUSD, while the Metal card costs $199/year and offers 3% cashback on up to $10,000 in annual spending, no foreign transaction fees and higher limits.

Outside the US, it is available in Argentina, Brazil, Canada, Colombia, the EEA, Mexico, Switzerland and the UK. The trade-off is that users take full responsibility for securing their own assets.

Best for: Existing MetaMask users who want to keep control of their keys.

The Nexo Card is a Mastercard issued by DiPocket UAB, a Lithuanian-licensed e-money institution (EMI). It offers two app-controlled modes: Credit Mode, which lets users borrow against their crypto without selling it, and Debit Mode.

Cashback depends on Nexo’s loyalty tier, portfolio balance, and card mode. Rewards are paid in NEXO tokens or BTC, with payouts changeable at any time. Rates can reach 2% in NEXO or 0.5% in BTC, although Nexo’s regional page lists up to 2% cashback for credit card holders.

The card is available to eligible users in selected European markets, including the EEA and UK.

Best for: European long-term holders who want liquidity without selling.

The Bybit Card is a Mastercard debit card linked to your Bybit account. In the EEA and Switzerland, it is issued by Moorwand Ltd and Harmoniie SAS, with a 0.5% FX fee on top of Mastercard’s rate and a 0.9% crypto conversion fee.

Availability is limited to selected markets, including the EEA, Switzerland, Australia, Argentina, Brazil, parts of Asia Pacific, and Mexico.

Rewards depend on spending tiers or VIP status, not a flat cashback rate. The advertised “up to 10%” applies only to top tiers.

Fees and limits vary by region, and cashback without VIP status can be minimal, particularly outside Europe. US users should consider alternatives.

Best for: Non-US Bybit traders who want to spend without leaving the crypto exchange.

RedotPay is a custodial Visa card for global stablecoin users, allowing crypto spending in over 100 countries.

It costs $10 for a virtual card or $100 for a physical one, with no monthly or annual fees, and supports major assets including USDT, USDC, BTC, ETH, BNB and SOL.

Standard pricing includes a 1% crypto-to-fiat conversion fee for USD transactions and an additional 1.2% FX markup.

Standard RedotPay accounts offer no ongoing cashback, relying on welcome bonuses and referral rewards. However, its optional RedotPay Pro membership offers 3% cashback on eligible Apple Pay and Google Pay purchases.

The card is unavailable in the US, Canada, China, Japan, South Korea, the Philippines and Russia.

Best for: Freelancers and remote workers paid in USDT outside the US.

Uphold relaunched its US debit card in October 2025, advertising up to 6% in XRP rewards, with additional benefits for direct deposit users. Actual rates vary by tier and conditions, with some sources citing up to 4%. The US offers Essential and Elite plans, both paying rewards exclusively in XRP.

Essential has no annual fee but charges $4.99 for a physical card, $2.95 per ATM withdrawal, and $1.50 in foreign transaction fees.

Elite costs $99.99 annually, includes a metal card, and waives Uphold ATM and foreign transaction fees.

Crypto-funded spending may involve spreads and taxable events. Availability varies by state, while UK users receive a separate program offering 1% cashback in GBP.

Best for: US users who want a multi-asset card and are comfortable earning XRP.

Ether.fi Cash is a non-custodial Visa card that connects DeFi assets to everyday spending. Users can pay directly with USDC or LiquidUSD, or borrow against their crypto without selling it.

The card combines debit-style direct payments with crypto-backed credit. Rewards reach 3% in USDC for most users and 4% for VIP members on the first $50,000.

It offers up to 3% cashback in USDC for most users, rising to 4% for VIP members on the first $50,000 spent. Fees and eligibility vary by tier and region, with some benefits requiring ETHFI staking.

Best for: experienced DeFi users already inside the ether.fi ecosystem.

The Bitpanda Card is a simple Visa debit card for EEA residents. It is available in all Eurozone countries except Cyprus, and requires a verified Bitpanda account and the mobile app.

The card offers 1% cashback on eligible crypto spending, access to more than 600 crypto assets, no monthly fee and no FX fees charged by Bitpanda, although Visa mark-ups may apply.

There are a few important exclusions: stablecoins, precious metals, Bitpanda Stocks and fiat balances do not qualify for cashback. Each payment also triggers a trade, meaning standard trading fees apply. ATM withdrawals cost 2%, with a minimum fee of €2.

Best for: Euro-area users who already invest with Bitpanda.

Gate Card is a custodial crypto debit card linked to your Gate account, available in virtual and physical Visa or Mastercard versions, depending on region. Compatible cards support Apple Pay and Google Pay, with instant virtual issuance.

Cashback ranges from 1% to 8%, depending on your VIP tier or monthly spending. Rewards are issued as points redeemable for USDT, GT and other supported assets, subject to monthly limits of $5–$400.

Fees vary by card, but the latest Blue and AI versions offer free issuance and no monthly fee, with a 0.9% top-up fee and 1.5–1.7% FX fee. Their limits reach $150,000 daily and $1 million monthly.

Level 2 KYC is required. The international service excludes certain jurisdictions, including the US, where a separate Gate US Visa card is available under different terms.

Best for: Existing Gate users who want crypto spending with tier-based rewards and are comfortable keeping funds on a custodial exchange.

The best crypto debit card depends on how you plan to use it, where you live, and which features matter most. Before applying, consider these five factors:

Not every crypto card works worldwide. Some are restricted to the US, EEA, UK, or selected countries. Check whether the provider supports residents of your country and whether the card offers the same features in your region.

Look beyond monthly and annual fees. Crypto conversion spreads, foreign exchange markups, ATM withdrawal charges, and card issuance costs can all affect how much you actually spend.

Compare the rewards you can realistically earn, not just the highest advertised percentage. Some providers require staking, paid subscriptions, or minimum spending levels to unlock better rates. Also check whether rewards are paid in cash, stablecoins, or volatile crypto assets.

Exchange-linked cards generally rely on custodial accounts, while self-custody products can allow users to retain control of their assets until payment. Understand who controls your funds and what happens if your account or wallet is compromised.

Some crypto cards offer prepaid spending, while others provide credit backed by crypto collateral. These products have different risks, repayment requirements, and potential tax implications. Make sure you understand which type you are applying for.

Traditional debit cards use money held in a bank account, while crypto debit cards are linked to cryptocurrency exchanges, digital wallets or stablecoin balances.

When making a payment, some crypto cards automatically convert your digital assets into fiat currency. Others let you spend stablecoins directly or borrow against your crypto holdings.

The main differences come down to funding, custody, fees and rewards. Crypto cards can offer cashback in digital assets and easier access to crypto funds, but may also involve conversion fees, additional account requirements and tax implications.

In some jurisdictions, spending crypto is treated as a taxable disposal. It’s worth checking the local tax rules before using crypto for everyday payments.

Crypto debit cards make it easier to use digital assets for everyday purchases, whether through crypto-funded payments, stablecoin spending or cashback rewards.

But the benefits aren’t always as good as they look. Conversion spreads, foreign transaction fees, subscription costs and staking requirements can eat into your rewards.

The best card depends on how you plan to use it. If low fees matter most, an exchange-linked card may be enough. If you prefer greater control over your assets or want to spend stablecoins, other options may be more suitable. For cashback, look beyond the advertised rate and factor in all associated costs.

Ultimately, choose a card that fits your spending habits, location and risk tolerance. Check the latest fees and terms, and don’t overlook potential tax implications.

A crypto debit card is a payment card linked to a cryptocurrency exchange account or digital wallet. It allows users to make purchases at merchants that accept its payment network, with crypto or stablecoins converted into fiat currency when required.

No. Availability depends on the card issuer, payment provider, and local regulations. Some cards are restricted to US residents, while others support selected European, Asian, or Latin American markets. Features and fees may also differ between regions.

Some crypto debit cards have no annual or monthly fees, but other costs may apply. These include crypto conversion spreads, foreign exchange fees, ATM withdrawal charges, issuance fees, and paid membership subscriptions.

It depends on the card. Many custodial cards convert cryptocurrency into fiat currency when a payment is processed. Some self-custody cards allow users to retain control of their assets until the transaction takes place, while crypto-backed credit products may allow spending without an immediate sale.

Tax treatment depends on your country and the type of reward. Spending appreciated cryptocurrency may trigger a taxable disposal, while cashback and promotional rewards can have different tax treatment. Consult the applicable tax rules in your jurisdiction.

#5173. Solana derivatives volume explodes 65% amid shrinking spot trading activity

GMTrade accounted for 77% of Solana’s tracked weekly perpetuals volume, as trading incentives raise questions about sustained demand.

Solana’s jump in tracked perpetuals trading is concentrated at GMTrade, a derivatives venue that accounts for about 77% of reported weekly turnover in DefiLlama’s Solana table.

Spot trading moved the other way, leaving a narrower demand picture than the derivatives headline suggests.

In the Nov. 10 snapshot, the Solana dashboard reports nearly $9 billion in seven-day perpetuals turnover, up 65.29% from the preceding week. GMTrade, listed by DefiLlama as GMX Solana, contributed nearly $7 billion, with a displayed weekly increase of 105%.

Over the same dashboard’s seven-day comparisons, spot decentralized exchange turnover fell 5% to $9.9 billion, and stablecoin market capitalization fell 4.38% to $14.5 billion.

November 10, 2026 · DefiLlama’s Solana classification. Pacifica’s Off Chain turnover is excluded. Perps turnover rose as spot turnover and stablecoin market capitalization fell.

GMTrade’s share of seven-day reported trade notional, calculated from rounded displayed totals.

GMTrade’s share of outstanding notional at the November 10 snapshot. This is a level, not a weekly growth rate.

Turnover counts trades; open interest counts outstanding notional. Neither measures fresh collateral or new SOL buying.

Shares use DefiLlama’s Solana classification, excluding Pacifica turnover classified Off Chain. Perps cover multiple underlying markets. Turnover is a seven-day flow; open interest and stablecoin market capitalization are stocks. The snapshot establishes no weekly open-interest trend or incentive causation.

Captured November 10, 2026 around 05:11 UTC. Rings use GMTrade/table ratios: 6.919/8.958 = 77.24% turnover; 174.87/235.13 = 74.37% open interest. Whole-percent labels are approximate, derived from rounded displayed inputs. The up arrow indicates direction only, not magnitude.

Shares use DefiLlama’s Solana classification, excluding Pacifica turnover classified Off Chain. Perps cover multiple underlying markets. Turnover is a seven-day flow; open interest and stablecoin market capitalization are stocks. The snapshot establishes no weekly open-interest trend or incentive causation.

DefiLlama’s Pacifica page attributes its total value locked (TVL) to Solana but classifies its $2.6 billion in weekly perpetuals turnover as “off-chain,” a turnover outside the Solana table.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

Dividing GMTrade’s reported weekly turnover by the table’s total gives an approximately 77% share. The rounded totals and growth rates also imply that GMTrade’s weekly increase was roughly as large as the entire table’s gain.

GMTrade’s trading documentation allows SOL exposure backed by either wrapped SOL or USDC collateral. A dollar of leveraged turnover cannot simply be counted as a dollar of new SOL buying.

GMTrade’s GT documentation describes points earned through trading, liquidity provision and referrals, with conditional treasury buybacks offering a route to USDC.

The announced Season 2 terms tie a referrer’s sellable quota to GT earned through referred traders’ trading, so earning points is different from receiving an unrestricted cash rebate.

The published fee documentation lists basic crypto-position opening or closing charges of 0.02% or 0.024%, depending on whether a trade improves the balance of longs and shorts. The Season 2 announcement also described a fee-structure change.

The incentives don't show how much of the weekly increase they caused, or how much trading would persist without them.

GMTrade’s connection to GMX extends beyond the label. GM Labs said in a Sept. 16 governance post that GMX Solana had been integrated into GMX, but GT points remain distinct from the GMX token.

In a Nov. 3 forum reply, contributor Jonezee said Solana-side buybacks were adding GMX to the staking rewards pool.

The Nov. 10 perps table shows nearly $174.9 million in GMTrade open interest, against $235.1 million for the table overall.

Open interest measures outstanding positions, while turnover measures the notional value traded during a period.

A weekly trend requires comparable observations over time, while stablecoin market capitalization measures the price-valued circulating balance. Falling spot turnover likewise measures activity.

The next test is whether GMTrade sustains its turnover across subsequent weeks, with open interest observed over matching periods. That would help distinguish repeat activity from a single weekly jump while the broader spot market remains quieter.

#5172. HTX Releases October Performance Report: Spot Liquidity Significantly Enhanced, APY Boosts Help Users Through a Warm Winter

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Since the start of Q4, the crypto market has continued to weaken amid volatility. Major asset prices have pulled back from their highs, and market participants have become more cautious. As the market cools, HTX has focused its efforts on solidifying its trading fundamentals and offering diverse yield generation pathways. In October, HTX saw a significant overall improvement in the market depth of its core spot trading pairs, with the 0.05% depth for the BTC/USDT pair increasing by 78%. Meanwhile, the platform’s total count  of stock trading assets grew to 307, with cumulative TradFi trading volume surpassing 7.5 billion USDT. At the end of October, HTX Earn launched the APY Boost Promotion as part of the HTX Winter Campaign, delivering stable yield options for users amid fluctuating market conditions.

Overall Spot Depth Enhancement, Ensuring Smoother Execution for Large-Volume Trades

In October, HTX continued to strengthen its collaboration with professional market makers, improving market-making support, order book depth, and the overall trading environment, which contributed to an overall improvement in the market depth of its core spot trading pairs. Taking BTC/USDT as an example, the pair’s 0.01% depth increased by 42% in October, while its 0.05% depth jumped by 78%. Deeper market depth ensures that orders of the same size have a smaller price impact, allowing large-volume trades to be executed closer to market price. For core assets like BTC, this means users can easily execute trades even during periods of severe market volatility.

Centered around the two core assets of BTC and ETH, HTX also rolled out a series of trading rewards in October, including trading challenges, fee rebates, trading lucky draws, and iPhone Duo theme activities, with the flagship trading challenge attracting over 10,000 participants.

Asset Matrix Continues to Expand, Stock Trading Assets Reach 307 Types

In October, HTX Futures launched 40 new assets, including 29 selected stocks and ETFs alongside 11 crypto assets. To date, the platform’s number of stock trading assets has grown to 307, covering core US stocks, major global indices and ETFs, biopharmaceuticals, energy infrastructure, and Asia-Pacific market leaders. Overall platform liquidity and user activity have both reached new highs.

This month’s new listings focused on sectors including AI computing power and hardware innovation, biopharmaceuticals and healthcare, mass consumption and high-dividend blue chips, as well as Asia-Pacific core markets and frontier technologies. Targets such as STMicroelectronics (STM), United Microelectronics (UMC), Synopsys (SNPS), Constellation Energy (CEG), Pfizer (PFE), Boeing (BA), Procter & Gamble (PG), McDonald’s (MCD), Starbucks (SBUX), Indonesia Index ETF (EIDO), and Taiyo Yuden (TAIYOYUDEN) were rolled out in succession, offering a balanced mix of growth-oriented tech stocks and defensive assets like consumer goods and pharmaceuticals.

As HTX continues to expand its asset offerings, cumulative TradFi trading volume has surpassed $7.5 billion, with $1.5 billion added in October alone.

#5171. Upbit lists HYPE – Can Hyperliquid narrow its 45x Spot trading gap?

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Hyperliquid has received another major boost, but the impact could be bigger than it initially appears.

Upbit has officially listed HYPE on their South Korean exchange. This is significant, as it means the largest crypto spot exchange in South Korea now holds HYPE. This gives traders in South Korea a massive new pool of liquidity. However, it’s Upbit’s dominance in South Korea that makes the listing even more significant.

According to FP Research, Upbit controlled a significant 68.6% of trading volume across the country’s top five major crypto exchanges in April 2026, much higher than Bithumb’s 19.5%. This gives HYPE access to South Korea’s largest crypto trading platform and a much wider pool of local investors.

Notably, though, Hyperliquid’s [HYPE] expansion into South Korea could be just the beginning.

Recently, Bitso, one of Latin America’s largest crypto exchanges, also added HYPE to its perpetual market. This is interesting since Upbit has a spot listing for HYPE. Put simply, Bitso increases HYPE’s exposure in derivatives, while Upbit provides increased exposure for HYPE to South Korean spot traders.

Together, these listings expand HYPE’s exposure into several new markets and trading segments. However, could the Upbit listing offer more value to Hyperliquid? On-chain activity shows that exposure to South Korea’s large spot market may attract some new buying interest and create increased spot liquidity to help reinvigorate the HYPE ecosystem.

Hyperliquid continues to lead the perp trading market, with competitors still struggling to close the gap.

According to DeFiLlama data, Hyperliquid saw more than $65 billion in perp volume this week alone, compared to Aster’s $11 billion. This shows how much of a commanding lead Hyperliquid has in derivatives. Meanwhile, Q4 perp volume has already reached nearly 50% of Q3’s $620 billion total, suggesting that trading activity on Hyperliquid remains strong despite broader market weakness.

Despite this, there is still plenty of growth left to come. Looking at the chart below, Hyperliquid has been averaging around $15 billion each quarter in spot trading volume this year. However, in Q3 2025 it hit $54 billion.

Looking at the gap between this and the derivatives volume in Q3 2025, which hit around $630 billion in perps, it is safe to say that Hyperliquid’s derivatives volume is almost 45x larger than Spot volume. In essence, Hyperliquid still depends heavily on derivatives activity to drive its on-chain momentum.

Against this backdrop, Upbit’s listing could put HYPE in a stronger position to close that gap. The opportunity to access South Korea’s big spot market opens up new buying opportunities, increasing spot liquidity, and helps diversify Hyperliquid’s trading activity beyond perpetual futures.

If this momentum continues, spot growth could become an important driver of the next phase of Hyperliquid’s ecosystem expansion.

Upbit’s 68.6% market share gives HYPE access to South Korea’s largest spot trading market.

With perp volume nearly 45 times larger than spot volume, Upbit’s listing could bring new buyers, boost spot activity and support HYPE’s growth.

#5170. Rothschild Investment Reveals XRP ETF Stake

Rothschild Investment LLC, the Chicago-based investment management firm, has filed its latest 13F with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), revealing its stake in the Bitwise XRP ETF.

Rothschild Investment’s filing, made on Nov. 10, indicates that the company has invested in 6,300 shares of the Bitwise XRP ETF.

Based on the information provided, these shares were worth $104,769 as of Sept. 30.

The investment in the Bitwise XRP ETF is listed under CUSIP 09174F107 in Rothschild Investment’s third-quarter report.

Interestingly, Rothschild Investment did not have any reported holdings of the XRP ETF in its previous quarterly filing, which indicates that the firm’s investment in the XRP ETF occurred in the third quarter of 2026.

The Bitwise XRP ETF, listed under the ticker XRP, was introduced in November 2025.

The ETF enables traditional investors to invest in the Ripple-linked cryptocurrency without needing to buy and hold XRP tokens themselves.

Although Rothschild Investment has invested in the XRP ETF, it is not a significant part of its overall portfolio.

The firm’s total portfolio value for 13F-reportable holdings is around $2.69 billion.

Rothschild Investment holds much larger stakes in Bitcoin and Ethereum investments.

When it comes to cryptocurrencies, Rothschild Investment’s largest holding is in the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF by BlackRock, where the company owns 40,188 shares worth around $1.9 million.

Additionally, Rothschild Investment reported holding $911,300 in the Grayscale Bitcoin Trust ETF and $335,160 in the Morgan Stanley Bitcoin Trust ETF.

Other Bitcoin-related investments include the Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust ETF ($125,113), VanEck Bitcoin ETF ($118,100), Bitwise Bitcoin ETF ($116,802) and Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund ($2,107).

In total, the seven Bitcoin investments represent around $3.51 million in reported holdings.

Rothschild Investment also has stakes in the Grayscale Ethereum Staking ETF worth $538,622 and the Bitwise Ethereum ETF worth $476,500.

The company also has a significant holding in the Bitwise Crypto Industry Innovators ETF, with 24,250 shares worth $615,223.

The firm owns $38,360 worth of shares in the Grayscale CoinDesk Crypto 5 ETF.

Finally, it has invested $69,900 in a Solana ETF.

Aside from cryptocurrency investment funds, Rothschild Investment has shares in publicly traded companies that are heavily involved in the digital asset space.

Michael Saylor’s Strategy is one such holding, with a $530,763 investment.

Other holdings include Coinbase Global ($86,681), Block ($125,060) and Riot Platforms ($42,980), a Bitcoin mining company.

#5169. Bitdeer Revenue Jumps 89% to $320.7M as AI Backlog Grows Despite Quarterly Loss

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

TL;DR: Bitdeer posted record third-quarter revenue of $320.7 million, up 89% year over year, while reporting a $125.5 million net loss. Its stated AI-cloud backlog approached $2.9 billion, highlighting demand potential but not revenue already earned or cash already collected.

Bitdeer has delivered one of the clearest examples yet of a Bitcoin mining business trying to transform itself into a provider of broader computing infrastructure. Its latest quarter brought record revenue and a sizable artificial-intelligence cloud order pipeline. It also remained deeply unprofitable under standard accounting measures.

In its November 10 third-quarter results announcement, the company reported $320.7 million in revenue, an 89% increase from the year-earlier period. Adjusted EBITDA rose to about $69.6 million, while the GAAP net loss reached approximately $125.5 million.

Those measures differ, and the gap requires careful reading. Management highlighted changes in the fair value of digital-asset-related borrowing, including a $54.6 million noncash item, as one factor in the accounting result.

The figure likely to attract the most attention is Bitdeer’s reported AI-cloud backlog of approximately $2.9 billion. A backlog represents contracted or expected future services under the company’s reporting definitions, rather than cash already received or recognized quarterly revenue.

The amount eventually converted into sales will depend on contract delivery, customer demand, capacity coming online and the terms attached to commitments. Investors should seek disclosures about timing and any conditions that could delay or reduce the total.

Nevertheless, a substantial backlog can signal customer interest for specialized infrastructure. That is particularly valuable in a business where constructing or equipping data centers involves significant upfront spending.

Bitdeer reported production of 3,855 Bitcoin during the quarter and said it held 47 Bitcoin at quarter-end. Those figures help distinguish operating output from Bitcoin retained on the balance sheet. Production can be high even if a firm sells most of the coins to fund operations, equipment or other projects.

The company also reported approximately $213.7 million in cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash. A cash balance should be considered alongside capital commitments, financing costs and planned expansion rather than treated as unencumbered profits from AI.

NewsBTC has reported on Riot’s decision to sell Bitcoin as it pursues major AI infrastructure contracts. The miners are pursuing different projects, but both illustrate a sector balancing near-term funding needs with investments that may generate future revenue.

Our coverage of Soluna and Bitdeer’s Texas infrastructure agreement adds a concrete example of why access to powered sites and commercial partnerships remains important as the competition for computing capacity grows.

Adjusted EBITDA may help investors evaluate operating performance before certain expenses and valuation changes. It is not identical to net income or free cash flow. A company can report a positive adjusted measure and still incur losses, financing costs and heavy investment requirements.

That is why the $125.5 million net loss deserves to stand alongside the $320.7 million revenue headline. Both are true, and neither alone gives a complete picture.

Bitdeer’s next reporting periods need to show when AI-cloud backlog turns into delivered services, how those services contribute to margins and how much capital they consume. Improvements in mining efficiency and power costs will also remain relevant.

The latest results point to striking revenue momentum and a potentially meaningful new business line. They do not yet demonstrate that the shift toward AI has resolved the financial volatility historically associated with Bitcoin mining.

#5167. What Trump Media’s $410M Q3 profits reveal about its Bitcoin exposure

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Trump Media & Technology Group is in the news today after reporting a $409.7 million Q3 profit, reversing a $238.1 million loss in Q2. Gains on digital assets and equity securities drove the turnaround.

At the time of writing, DJT traded at $4.10, with its shares closing at $4.06 on 9th November, up 1.75% before the earnings release.

Trump Media recorded $496.1 million in combined gains on digital assets and equity securities. The largest contribution was a $200.8 million unrealized gain on Bitcoin [BTC] pledged for its Options strategy. By quarter-end, the company had pledged 11,385.20 BTC for that strategy.

Another $107.5 million came from unrealized gains on Bitcoin and Cronos [CRO] holdings.

Equity securities added about $118 million in realized and unrealized gains.

After derivatives losses and other investment items, it reported $60 million in net investment income. CFO Phillip Juhan linked that investment income to a rise in BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT).

This reflects the 42% increase in IBIT’s closing share price to roughly $47 on September 30th, from roughly $33 on June 30th.

Trump Media also used proceeds from a partial sale of its IBIT holdings to buy 4,359 BTC during the quarter.

The next test for Trump Media’s Bitcoin [BTC] holdings can come from its debt. Holders of up to $1 billion in convertible notes could demand cash repayment on 30th November.

According to Interim CEO Kevin McGurn, the company favors using cash and credit and wants to “preserve as much of our Bitcoin as possible.” Management also clarified that the amount holders would request remains uncertain.

Bitcoin also made up about half of the $718.5 million in collateral backing the notes at quarter-end. Bitcoin-related securities and restricted cash made up the rest.

On 5th November, two transfers moved about 4,259 BTC to Crypto.com from wallets Arkham labeled as note collateral. The total was close to the 4,260.73 BTC listed in the filing.

The repayment deadline falls before Trump Media’s shareholder vote on the proposed TAE Technologies merger on 14th December. TAE drew another $100 million from Trump Media on 7th October, after the quarter-end cash snapshot.

Chainlink sees a death cross approaching on the chart, with a solid possibility of an aggravation of the current state of affairs on the market. LINK is trading at around $10.49 at the moment, moving below every moving average on the daily chart.

The 50 EMA is rapidly diving down and most likely to cross the 100 EMA sooner rather than later. The 50 EMA sits near $11.70 right now, while the 100 EMA is around $11.40, so the gap between them is getting thin.

EMAs are also converging – an important sign that might cause some worrying certainly. The longest moving average on the chart, at around $11, was lost in early November, and LINK hasn't been able to get back above it since.

Luckily, volume is descending, so there's a good chance that things will stabilize rather than degrade from here. Daily volume in November is visibly lower than during the sell-off at the end of October, which is a good sign.

RSI is moving sideways, in a tunnel around 50, so the situation is, in some sense, neutral for the asset. The indicator hasn't made any sharp moves since mid-October, and the market isn't anywhere near the oversold zone.

A strong uptick in volume here would be beneficial. Daily volume in November is among the lowest on the chart, so buyers aren't really showing up even at these prices.

The lack of catalyst is the larger problem: ADA has no traction around it and there's certainly a chance that it won't appear in the foreseeable future.

Fundamentally, ADA had no breakthroughs recently apart from the foundation's support of Cosmos IBC transition to Linux Foundation governance. It's more of an interoperability and institutional infrastructure related development.

Strategy had said it would not issue STRC below that price, but its November 9 disclosure reported no STRC sales under its at-the-market offering program.

The allocation shows where the week’s financing went. Of $283.8 million in net proceeds from MSTR common shares, $188.3 million funded STRC repurchases, $81.9 million funded Bitcoin purchases and $13.6 million went to USD Cash, according to the weekly financing update.

That put about two-thirds of the new common-stock money into buying back preferred shares. Less than a third went into Bitcoin. STRC’s market-price recovery had yet to become reported STRC ATM financing within that week.

Strategy’s November 2–8 MSTR proceeds went mostly to repurchasing preferred shares. No STRC ATM sales were reported for the week.

STRC buybacks received 2.3 times the common-stock proceeds allocated to Bitcoin.

Strategy’s July 27 policy announcement said the company would not issue STRC below $100. It also described a long-term objective of healthy, sustained trading near that level. The issuance and dividend policies were statements of intent that could change.

Strategy receives new equity capital when it sells shares and collects proceeds. In a secondary-market trade, a buyer instead pays another investor for an existing share. The market price and the issuer’s financing proceeds therefore describe separate transactions.

For November 2–8, the reported financing came from selling 2,051,348 MSTR shares. That share-sales figure includes shares sold but not yet settled as of November 6.

CryptoSlate’s November 5 coverage described renewed STRC financing as a possibility and included an unconfirmed tracker estimate that issuance might have financed 191 BTC. The subsequent weekly disclosure reports no STRC ATM sales for the period containing November 4.

Strategy bought 1,036 BTC for $81.9 million during the week, at an average $79,012 per coin including fees and expenses. Its Bitcoin purchase disclosure expressly identifies MSTR sale proceeds as the funding source.

Bitcoin purchases absorbed 28.9% of the common-stock proceeds. STRC repurchases took 66.3%, or about 2.3 times the Bitcoin allocation, while USD Cash received 4.8%. That makes the buyback program a substantial competing use of newly raised capital.

It also changes the mix of claims on the company. Issuing MSTR expands the common-share base, while repurchasing STRC reduces preferred claims. Strategy bought back 1,887,464 STRC shares during November 2–8.

The company’s July policy described discounted repurchases as a way to reduce future preferred dividend requirements. That gives the spending an economic purpose alongside its immediate cash cost. The eventual dividend savings depend on future rates and declarations.

The policy also anticipated a greater repurchase pace at deeper discounts, tapering as STRC approached $100. It left decisions subject to liquidity, market conditions and capital-allocation priorities.

The preceding week also paired MSTR fundraising with STRC repurchases, but disclosed a different funding route. In its November 2 filing, Strategy reported $164 million in MSTR proceeds: $65.5 million funded Bitcoin purchases and $98.5 million went to USD Cash. It separately used $208.2 million of USD Cash for STRC repurchases.

For November 2–8, the company explicitly assigned MSTR proceeds directly to the buybacks. The comparison shows a change in the disclosed funding allocation, with common-stock sales financing Bitcoin purchases in both weeks.

At November 8, USD Cash stood at $146.2 million, alongside a separate $4.77 billion reserve for dividends and interest. Strategy used $21.1 million of that reserve to pay preferred dividends during the week.

The next financing development depends on reported issuer sales and the use of their proceeds. STRC’s return to $100 provided a market-price milestone; the November 2–8 allocation shows that MSTR issuance supplied the disclosed money for both Bitcoin accumulation and preferred-share repurchases.

#5164. eToro Q3 Profit Drops 74% as Crypto Trading Activity Slows

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

TL;DR: eToro reported third-quarter net income of about $15 million, down from $57 million a year earlier, as crypto-related activity weakened. Its funded-account base continued to grow, highlighting the difference between attracting customers and generating trading revenue from them in any particular quarter.

A trading platform can gain users even when the market becomes less profitable to trade. That tension runs through eToro’s latest financial results, which showed weaker quarterly earnings despite an expanding customer base.

According to the company’s November 10 earnings release, third-quarter net income was approximately $15 million, a decline of about 74% from $57 million in the comparable period. Net contribution came to around $186 million, down 13% year over year, with lower cryptocurrency trading activity contributing to the drop.

At the same time, eToro reported 4.39 million funded accounts, an increase of 18%, and assets under administration of approximately $20.8 billion. It also announced a $250 million share repurchase authorization.

Brokerage and trading businesses earn revenue from a mix of activity, product pricing and other services. When customers trade less frequently, a growing account base may not immediately offset the effect. The relationship is particularly visible in crypto, where transaction volumes can shift quickly as market sentiment changes.

That is why the funded-account figure and the net-contribution figure should be assessed together. One shows a measure of customer acquisition and retention; the other gives more insight into the contribution earned from services in the quarter.

Assets under administration are also distinct from eToro’s own cash and corporate assets. They reflect client-related asset values that can be affected by price movements as well as client activity.

Lower crypto activity at one trading platform does not prove digital assets are in a long-term decline. Users may trade through different venues, switch into other asset classes or simply become less active during a choppy period. The business may also earn different amounts from different types of orders.

Still, eToro’s numbers offer an operating-business perspective on the volatility seen in public-market crypto demand. NewsBTC has been tracking recent Bitcoin ETF outflows as well as uneven demand for spot Ether funds. ETF subscriptions and brokerage transaction revenues are separate metrics, but both help describe how investors are participating in the market.

A fall in net contribution can also reflect conditions in noncrypto products. Readers should avoid attributing every change in a diversified platform’s results to Bitcoin prices alone.

The $250 million repurchase authorization gives eToro permission to buy back shares under its program, subject to the company’s terms. It is not proof that the full amount was repurchased on November 10, nor does it guarantee future share-price gains.

Repurchases can alter the share count and capital allocation over time, but their effect depends on execution price, cash available and how the company balances other investments. They are best evaluated alongside earnings quality and strategic spending.

Investors should watch whether funded-account growth leads to sustained activity and improved net contribution in subsequent quarters. The product mix matters: strength in equities or other services could help offset a quieter crypto market, while increased marketing and operating costs could limit the benefit.

For crypto observers, the report is a reminder that adoption and profitability do not always move together. eToro gained funded accounts, but the softer trading environment made it harder to translate that scale into quarterly profit.

#5162. Why Is Bitcoin Down Today? Key Factors Behind BTC’s Slide Toward $73K

Home » Bitcoin (BTC) » Why Is Bitcoin Down Today? Key Factors Behind BTC’s Slide Toward $73K

Bitcoin’s decline comes as market sentiment weakens, raising questions about whether the latest pullback could deepen.

Bitcoin fell to $73,770 on November 11, with several warning signals emerging across financial markets as pressure on the cryptocurrency mounted.

The world’s largest cryptocurrency dropped 1.6% over the past 24 hours. BTC briefly fell to $72,740 on November 10 before recovering some ground.

Meanwhile, the broader crypto market is showing signs of growing anxiety. The Crypto Fear & Greed Index has fallen to 35, placing sentiment firmly in the Fear zone. This marks a further deterioration from last week’s and last month’s reading of 46, which indicated Neutral sentiment.

So, what is driving Bitcoin lower? Four developments are putting pressure on the cryptocurrency, with unexpectedly high US inflation emerging as the biggest concern.

The biggest pressure on Bitcoin price comes from the latest US inflation figures.

October’s Consumer Price Index (CPI) increased 0.4%, exceeding economists’ expectations of 0.3%, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy prices, also came in hotter than expected, rising 0.3% against forecasts of 0.2%.

The figures have raised concerns that the Federal Reserve could increase interest rates in December rather than ease monetary policy.

According to CME Group’s FedWatch tool, interest rate futures now imply an 88.5% probability of a 25-basis-point rate hike next month.

That shift matters for Bitcoin because higher interest rates generally make riskier assets less attractive. When borrowing costs rise and safer investments offer better returns, investors may reduce exposure to speculative assets such as cryptocurrencies.

Another source of weakness is the persistent withdrawal of money from US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

These funds have recorded approximately $2.15 billion in net outflows since October 30, according to SoSoValue data.

The situation became particularly concerning last Friday, when US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded approximately $696 million in single-day outflows, their largest daily withdrawal since January, according to Glassnode.

“Only two days in the past year saw larger outflows, and both came before price fell further,” Glassnode noted in a post on X.

ETF investors are selling bitcoin:native again.US spot ETFs saw $696M of net outflows on Friday, the largest single day since January.Only two days in the past year saw larger outflows, and both came before price fell further. A return to steady inflows would ease that… pic.twitter.com/q9mnj4FWFf

The analytics firm added that a return to consistent inflows would help ease the selling pressure.

The sell-off has also been amplified by forced liquidations in the crypto derivatives market.

More than $742 million worth of crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours, according to CoinGlass data. Around $583 million came from long positions, meaning traders who had bet on rising prices.

Broader financial markets are also becoming less supportive of Bitcoin.

The US Dollar Index, which tracks the dollar against six major currencies, rose 0.1% to 102.30, nearing its highest level since October 29. Meanwhile, the yield on the US 10-year Treasury note moved closer to 5%.

Experts agree that both trends can weigh on Bitcoin. A stronger dollar and higher bond yields make traditional investments more attractive, giving investors less reason to take risks on assets like cryptocurrencies.

Derivatives analytics platform CoinGlass recently flagged $74,400 as a key level for BTC, warning that a sustained breakdown beneath it would confirm a bearish bias.

Additionally, Bitcoin recently closed its fifth consecutive red weekly candle while slipping below its 50-week moving average at the similar levels.

Analysts warned that failing to quickly reclaim this key moving average makes a drop toward $70,000 highly probable for Bitcoin.

As such, Schwartz has sold off nearly all his previous Bitcoin and Ethereum holdings.

It is not clear when he made the bulk of his sales or how much he made from them.

#5160. Exodus Reports $8.3M Quarterly Loss as Wallet Platform Expands Payments Business

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

TL;DR: Exodus reported third-quarter revenue of around $32.5 million, up 7%, while swinging to an $8.3 million net loss from a profit a year earlier. The wallet company’s expansion into payments and card infrastructure adds a new commercial opportunity but also increases the importance of integration costs and execution.

Exodus built its brand around software that helps people hold and exchange digital assets without relying on a traditional centralized exchange account. Its latest results show that running a wallet business at scale now involves more than downloads and token swaps.

In its November 9 third-quarter report, Exodus said revenue reached about $32.5 million, an increase of roughly 7% year over year. The company nevertheless recorded a net loss of approximately $8.3 million, compared with a net profit of about $17 million a year earlier.

The difference between higher revenue and weaker net income points to costs and accounting items that require as much attention as transaction volume.

Exodus reported around 1.4 million monthly active users and approximately 1.4 million quarterly funded users, reflecting the scale of its consumer product. Those are company-defined measures and may overlap; they should not be added together to imply a larger distinct customer base.

The company also cited roughly $1.1 billion in quarterly swap volume. Transaction volume measures value moved through a service; it is not the same as revenue or profit. The share retained by a platform depends on fees, execution arrangements and the costs of providing the service.

This is a useful distinction across the wallet industry. A product can support heavy activity without retaining a large percentage of the value exchanged. Increased usage can even create more customer-service, compliance and technical costs.

Exodus has been extending its role in the infrastructure around digital payments. Its recent company updates describe a combination involving Baanx and Monavate and a growing emphasis on card and payment services. It has also referenced around 1.6 million active cards and substantial payment volume in the broader business context.

Payment services offer a way to make digital assets useful for routine spending rather than only investment and exchange. But building or combining regulated payment operations brings operational work: issuing relationships, settlement partners, compliance programs, fraud controls and support obligations.

NewsBTC previously covered Visa’s work on stablecoin treasury and settlement infrastructure. Exodus operates in a different part of the market, yet both stories show businesses looking for ways to make digital value move through established financial channels.

Likewise, the growing attention paid to tokenized securities infrastructure reflects a wider focus on how blockchain assets connect with ordinary financial workflows. Neither development should be mistaken for proof that Exodus’s specific payment plans will succeed.

Management cited increased general and administrative spending among the pressures on the quarter. As a company moves from a comparatively focused software product toward a broader financial-services platform, staffing, oversight and integration costs can rise before new lines generate consistent returns.

That does not make the strategy inherently flawed. It means the outcome will depend on whether additional services create more durable recurring earnings than they cost to build and operate.

The useful measures in future results will include transaction and card activity, net revenue retained from those services, the cost of operating the expanded business and whether losses narrow. Users and investors should also pay attention to security, custody arrangements and regulatory disclosures as more payment services are introduced.

Exodus is showing modest revenue growth alongside a more expensive operating model. The next several quarters will help determine whether its payments ambitions create a stronger business or simply add complexity to an already competitive wallet market.

#5159. AI chatbot for new mothers shows zero postpartum mental health gain

At 12 months, Rosie users showed no significant anxiety or depression advantage over a monthly children's book program.

Access to Rosie, an AI chatbot for maternal health, showed no statistically significant anxiety or depression benefit at 12 months compared with a monthly children's book program in a 400-person randomized trial.

The study, published Nov. 4 in JAMA Network Open, tested access to health advice among pregnant and postpartum participants with generally low starting symptom scores.

Rosie was designed to answer maternal and infant health questions, offer personalized guidance, and provide reminders and educational support. A clinical social worker reviewed distress alerts, contacted participants, and provided resources, so the intervention included human support alongside the chatbot.

Researchers assigned 200 participants to each group. The US study enrolled English-speaking people aged 14 or older who were pregnant or parenting an infant younger than six months and identified as members of racial or ethnic minoritized groups.

Enrollment ran from October 2023 through December 2024, with follow-up completed in December 2025.

The primary measures were self-reported anxiety symptoms on the GAD-7 questionnaire and depression symptoms on the PHQ-9 questionnaire. The 12-month analyses included 361 participants for anxiety and 362 for depression.

The adjusted difference between the chatbot and control groups was 0.10 points for anxiety, with a 95% confidence interval of -0.77 to 0.96. For depression, it was -0.23 points, with an interval of -1.05 to 0.59.

Both intervals include zero, leaving uncertainty about the size and direction of any underlying effect. The trial established neither a clear benefit nor equivalence between the approaches.

US, English-speaking pregnant/postpartum participants from racial or ethnic minoritized groups, with generally low baseline symptoms. 400 randomized; endpoint samples: anxiety 361, depression 362. Outcomes were self-reported. Rosie included incentives and human support; both groups could contact staff.

Participants received small payments for questions and book rewards for the most active users. The control group received one children's board book per month for a year, and both groups could communicate with study staff.

Those conditions limit how directly the findings translate to routine chatbot use.

Participants generally began with low symptom scores. Among those with available baseline responses, the median anxiety score was 2, and the median depression score was 3. About 11.1% and 9.5% of the participants, respectively, met the study's moderate-to-severe threshold.

Self-reported health outcomes are another limitation, and the authors urged caution about secondary and exploratory findings.

Rosie, delivered with incentives and human backup to this population, showed no statistically significant 12-month advantage on the two primary mental-health measures. Whether other AI interventions or different clinical populations would yield different results remains open.

#5158. Coinbase, Kalshi, Kraken parent seek to back CFTC in stock perps fight

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Some of crypto’s biggest names are lining up behind the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) in court. The fight is over whether Americans get to trade perpetual futures on individual stocks.

On the 9th of November, Coinbase, Kalshi, Kraken’s parent Payward, DRW Holdings, Jump Trading and Paradigm asked a federal judge to let them file a brief backing the CFTC.

What’s the fight about? The Capital Markets Alliance Association (CMAA) sued to undo the CFTC’s approval of single-stock perpetual futures.

These six companies think the CFTC got it right.

In the brief (shared by Coinbase’s legal representative Molly Abraham), they argue these products already fit under existing US futures laws. Thing is, the judge isn’t leaning their way so far.

Just days earlier, the court said the CFTC likely “exceeded its statutory authority” by letting these contracts trade as security futures.

So they’re jumping in while they’re behind.

Last week, the CFTC said stock perps could trade on US-regulated exchanges for the first time. Days later, the CMAA sued. This is a new trade group, and its members include Cboe and Citadel Securities.

The argument being made is that a contract with no end date isn’t a future. It’s a security-based swap, which puts it mainly under the SEC. It would also have to come with stricter limits on retail trading.

Not everyone agrees. Per Coinbase and team, nothing says a security future has to expire. This would keep these contracts under shared CFTC and SEC watch.

Judge Valerie Caproni is leaning toward the trade group for now. She said these look more like swaps. But she didn’t stop trading, since the group couldn’t show it faced urgent, lasting harm.

So stock perps stay live, for now. The trade group’s next filing is due on the 10th.

After invite-only early access, the desktop app from the team behind Brevis is now open to anyone on Mac and Windows.

HONG KONG, November 11, 2026: Arca, a new desktop app from the team behind Brevis, opened to the public today. Arca pays people for the AI sessions they’d otherwise throw away. It finds the session history their AI tools already keep on their computer, lets them choose which sessions to submit, strips sensitive details on the device before anything is uploaded, and pays for the sessions that are approved. Starting today, anyone can sign up with an email address, with no invite and no waitlist.

Much of today’s knowledge work runs through AI tools. People steer a model through a task, correcting it, throwing out what fails and keeping what holds up. Every one of those sessions leaves a detailed record of real work: the back-and-forth, the dead ends, the fix that finally worked. These records pile up by the thousands on people’s computers, and once the window closes, they’re worth nothing to the person who did the work. Arca gives that work a value.

Arca works with the AI tools people already use, including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Claude Desktop. After installing the app, users see the sessions Arca has found on their machine, past ones included. They pick a session to upload, and Arca anonymises it on their computer before it leaves, then returns a quote range. Users either confirm, which sends the session to review, or withdraw, in which case the upload is deleted. Approved sessions are paid weekly.

Arca only reads sessions that are already on the user’s computer, and it lists everything it finds. Nothing uploads in the background, and nothing leaves the device until the user picks a session and confirms. Before a session is uploaded, Arca strips names, file paths, account details and keys, and further anonymising runs on Arca’s side.

“Every AI session is a record of real thinking and real work, and until now the person who did that work got nothing for it,” said Michael, co-founder and CEO of Brevis. “Arca lets people see what their sessions are worth and decide for themselves what to share. We opened it in small batches first to get the experience right. Today it’s open to everyone.”

Arca is built for anyone who does real work with AI, from code to contract reviews, research and long working conversations. Sessions with Claude Opus and Fable, and with the latest GPT models in Codex, qualify today, with more to come. Very short sessions don’t qualify, and every submission is reviewed before it pays. Users can connect GitHub to strengthen their profile, which can raise the value of their sessions, but it isn’t required.

Arca carries the principle behind Brevis’s verifiable computing work into a new domain: things you can verify are worth more than things you have to trust.

Arca first opened on October 13 in invite-only early access, admitting users in small batches. With today’s launch, the invite requirement is gone. Users sign up with an email address or a Google account and can start right away. Arca is free to use and available now for Mac and Windows at arca.market.

Through November 30, the Arca Launch Challenge adds $10,000 in prizes on top of regular payouts for approved sessions.

#5155. Does Holding Crypto Put Your Social Security at Risk in 2026?

Home » Cryptopedia » Does Holding Crypto Put Your Social Security at Risk in 2026?

Understanding SSA rules on digital assets and how ABLE accounts can legally protect your benefits.

Short answer: It depends on the type of Social Security benefits you receive.

If you receive Social Security Retirement or SSDI benefits, owning Bitcoin or other crypto generally won’t affect your monthly Social Security payments, as both of these programs don’t have asset limits.

However, if you receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI), things are different. The Social Security Administration (SSA) counts crypto as a resource. If your total countable assets exceed $2,000 for an individual, your SSI benefits could be reduced or suspended.

Note: The figures above are taken from the SSA 2026 COLA fact sheet and the SSA’s ABLE spotlight.

Much of the online confusion around cryptocurrency and Social Security stems from mixing up earned benefits with means-tested benefits:

The Social Security Administration’s (SSA) official Program Operations Manual System (POMS SI 01140.208 and SI 00830.102) outlines explicit rules for digital assets:

Consider an SSI recipient who holds $1,500 in a traditional bank account and receives $600 worth of Bitcoin as a gift:

Crypto’s market volatility introduces a unique risk for benefit compliance. If your wallet balance sits at $1,800 on October 25th, but a market surge pushes its dollar value to $2,200 on November 1st, you are technically over the SSI resource limit for November.

SSA requires beneficiaries to report changes in resources by the 10th day of the month following the change. Thus, logically, recipients must maintain accurate exchange statements, wallet screenshots, and transaction logs to verify historical values.

If you receive SSI and wish to save money without breaching resource caps, an Achieving a Better Life Experience (ABLE) account provides a legal shield:

Note: Check whether your state’s specific ABLE plan offers crypto-indexed investment options before transferring digital assets into the program.

Yes. Under the Access to Financial Institutions (AFI) program and POMS SI 01140.208 reporting procedures, SSA verifies asset balances. Recipients are legally required to disclose digital exchange accounts and self-custody wallet addresses. Failing to report crypto can lead to overpayment penalties or fraud investigations.

Cashing out converts one countable resource (crypto) into another (cash). The total dollar amount still applies to your $2,000 resource limit. However, if you sell at a profit, any capital gains can be counted as unearned income in the month realized, which could reduce or eliminate that month’s SSI check before the cash is evaluated as a resource the following month.

No. Transferring or gifting assets for less than fair market value to satisfy the $2,000 limit triggers a transfer penalty. SSA can impose a period of ineligibility for up to 36 months depending on the value of the crypto given away.

Not directly as coins. ABLE accounts only accept contributions in U.S. dollars. To move crypto into an ABLE account, you must first liquidate the cryptocurrency into cash and deposit the cash into the ABLE account (up to the $20,000 annual limit for 2026). Once inside, the funds are shielded up to $100,000 from the SSI resource test.

#5153. Binance hack funds worth $430K traced through 6 NEAR memecoins – Report

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

The tremors of the Binance exploit are still being felt, as, according to a recent report by Elliptic, the North Korean hackers are using a new method to launder stolen cryptocurrency by creating their own worthless meme tokens.

Instead of transferring stolen funds directly between wallets, they are routing them through decentralized exchange (DEX) liquidity pools. This is done to make it harder and more time-consuming for investigators to trace where the money goes.

This time, the hacker started by creating a new cryptocurrency token using publicly available token-launch platforms. Soon after that, they paired this token with a legitimate asset, such as Near Protocol [NEAR] or a stablecoin, in a liquidity pool on a DEX.

Providing more insights on the matter, the report added,

Each of the six NEAR tokens carries a logo in classic meme coin style…The names follow meme coin habits too, from a crude joke (FUK) to an echo of the “-INU” dog coins (SINU).

They then used wallets holding stolen funds to buy the newly created token.

Finally, another set of wallets sold those tokens back into the same pool and withdrew legitimate crypto assets. Now since the liquidity pool sat between the buying and selling wallets, there was no direct transfer of stolen funds between them.

According to this blockchain analytics firm, this technique was previously observed during the laundering of funds stolen from the Bybit hack in 2025.

At that time, too, the wrongdoers had moved at least $24 million through a worthless token created on the Tron [TRON] network.

The same approach has now appeared as Elliptic identified its use across TRON [TRX], NEAR, and Solana [SOL]. In fact, between 5th and 7th November, hackers created at least six memecoins on NEAR, including FUK, OLCCL, MEILI, MMLI, DABI, and SINU, with each token costing approximately 25 NEAR, or $90.

In this, around 117,000 NEAR, worth approximately $430,000, passed through these six tokens. The transactions followed a similar pattern, with tokens experiencing heavy trading within hours of creation before being abandoned. In some cases, the remaining liquidity was also withdrawn.

This followed the FBI attributing the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking group. All this while, North Korean cyber-espionage group Kimsuky is increasingly using AI tools to strengthen its cyberattacks.

The governance proposal sets out initial stablecoin credit lines from Aave's Core Hub liquidity pool of $8 million each for USDT and USDC, $1 million for GHO, and $2 million each for USDG and RLUSD.

A separate liquidity pool, the Babylon Hub, would let liquidity providers choose exposure to native Bitcoin collateral, with its own limits.

Babylon targets mainnet for late 2026, subject to change and confirmation. It says deployment will start with restrictions on participants and volume, with a schedule and staged rollout plan still to follow. Its current FAQ directs users to a public testnet and gives a fourth-quarter mainnet target.

Keeping the underlying BTC on Bitcoin does not remove liquidation or settlement risk. The Ethereum collateral record would be a transfer-restricted ERC-20 accounting unit, and a borrower could still lose vault collateral through liquidation.

The design also retains a role for Wrapped Bitcoin (WBTC). Under the permissionless liquidation route, BTCVaultSwap would borrow WBTC from an Aave Hub to settle immediately with liquidators.

Permissioned arbitrageurs would later repay that debt and redeem the underlying BTC over several days, as LlamaRisk's assessment describes.

The proposed Core Hub draw cap for that settlement venue is 100 WBTC, separate from the stablecoin lending lines. Permissioned actors can also liquidate and redeem vaults directly without drawing Hub liquidity, although fees or borrower compensation can still require WBTC.

Liquidation seizes whole vaults, even when clearing the debt requires less than a vault's full BTC value, and the borrower receives discounted compensation for that remainder in wrapped BTC.

Prospective borrowers still need final AIP approval and a confirmed rollout schedule before this market moves from governance backing to mainnet access.
