#5151. ARK Invest Trims Block and Bullish Positions as Bitcoin ETF Outflows Continue

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

TL;DR: Disclosed ARK Invest trading activity points to sales of shares in crypto-linked companies Block and Bullish alongside changes elsewhere in its portfolios. A fund manager selling shares is not the same as investors redeeming money from a spot Bitcoin ETF, and the trades should not be treated as a categorical forecast for crypto prices.

Crypto markets generate several types of selling headlines, but they do not all describe the same thing. One involves investors moving money into or out of exchange-traded products. Another involves a fund manager changing which companies it owns inside a portfolio. ARK Invest’s latest trade disclosures belong to the second category.

ARK’s trade-notification service provides information about purchases and sales by its exchange-traded funds. Reporting of the November 9 trades indicates reductions in shares of Block and Bullish, both businesses tied to the wider digital-asset economy.

Trade data published for the session should be checked against the original ARK notification for exact fund allocations and amounts. Public summaries can combine activity across several ETFs, while dollar-value estimates change with the share price used for calculation.

A growth-oriented fund might sell shares to rebalance position weights, manage liquidity, fund purchases of other holdings or respond to company-specific developments. A share sale alone cannot reveal which of those motives dominated.

For that reason, it would be a mistake to describe ARK’s selling as proof that the manager has abandoned Bitcoin. The sale may reflect a view on the risk and valuation of individual equities rather than the future value of the underlying cryptocurrency.

Block’s exposure to digital assets is also different from Bullish’s. Their revenue drivers, regulation and business models are not interchangeable merely because both are routinely grouped under the label ‘crypto stock.’ Investors comparing them need to look beyond the common theme.

NewsBTC has recently tracked sizable outflows from US spot Bitcoin funds and earlier daily Bitcoin ETF withdrawals. Those figures measure net investor flows into or out of specific products, rather than an ETF manager switching between equity holdings.

Even within ETF reporting, transactions can be misunderstood. Selling shares in a listed company held by an actively managed ETF does not necessarily imply the ETF itself suffered a redemption. Likewise, a Bitcoin ETF net outflow does not automatically show why an individual investor chose to redeem.

Those distinctions become especially important in a market where the same financial firm may own Bitcoin directly, operate a fund holding mining or exchange equities, and manage entirely different technology-sector positions.

Shares of trading venues, payment companies and miners are often affected by crypto prices but can also move on earnings results, borrowing costs and capital spending. A mining company pursuing AI infrastructure may be valued on its power contracts as much as its Bitcoin output. A brokerage might add accounts while earning less from crypto transactions.

That mixture means crypto-equity portfolio changes sometimes convey a different message from spot-token trading activity. They are better read as part of ongoing active management than as standalone signals to buy or sell a coin.

The strongest verifiable facts are the securities traded, the direction of the trade and the number of shares reported for each fund. If later reporting establishes exact price-weighted values, those should be dated and described as estimates where appropriate.

ARK’s trading notices offer a window into portfolio decisions, not a complete explanation of motive. Their value for readers comes from knowing precisely what changed and avoiding the temptation to translate every share sale into a broad claim about the Bitcoin market.

#5150. Deutsche Bank Opens Digital Asset Custody to Paying Institutional Clients

Deutsche Bank opens up digital asset custody to paying institutional clients. The service includes storage, user experience improvements, and accessibility via the bank's own gateways. The bank announced the launch on November 11, as DB's official website reveals.

This is an improvement in the field of institutional adoption, even though it comes at a time when it might be unwarranted. The market is experiencing serious issues and constant outflows from both retail and institutional investors.

Surprisingly, the bank can provide both warm and cold storage options available directly through DB's infrastructure. According to the landing page, the platform will provide key storage via Hardware Security Modules. Access goes through Autobahn, the bank's own multi-channel gateway.

Compliance will also be handled by Deutsche Bank. Initially, the service will focus on core functions: custody of digital assets and transfers, with further capabilities planned.

The Asian market has yet to receive similar treatment. For now, the service is available in the EU, operating out of DB AG Frankfurt. An expansion to Asia is reportedly planned for 2027, though the details are yet to be confirmed.

Additionally, DB announced support for euro stablecoins such as EURC and EURAU, in addition to BTC, ETH, and USDC. This is an attempt to promote the adoption of EU-issued stablecoins as part of a strategy aimed at moving away from USDT dominance. EURAU is issued by AllUnity, a joint venture that includes DWS, the asset manager majority-owned by Deutsche Bank.

Self-custody or banks: that is the real question here. Industry experts such as Bloomberg's ETF analyst Eric Balchunas suggest that self-custody has been a worse option and that a custodian with funds protection and insurance is a better option for regular investors. Even Binance founder CZ admitted after the Ledger incident that self-custody comes with extra responsibilities.

Back in August, a Coldcard exploit drained 1,816 BTC from more than 5,000 cold-storage addresses, according to Fortune.

However, it puts some pressure on those who might receive their funds from grey sources. Unfortunately for them, a bank custodian creates another barrier, as every deposit has to go through the bank's compliance checks.

#5149. 14 companies sold 108,247 Bitcoin in 2026, but here’s why it’s not what it looks like!

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Companies that bought Bitcoin [BTC] to hold are starting to sell some of it. What’s worse is that they’re not the only ones facing the heat.

According to data from Lookonchain, 14 public companies have sold 108,247 BTC worth $8.08 billion in 2026.

MARA has sold the most by far, about 40,581 BTC for $3.03B, at an average of $74,446 per coin. Riot Platforms was next with figures of 20,264 BTC. That’s worth $1.51 billion, at about $73,231 each.

Together, these two make up half of the total.

Bitdeer was in third, with an estimated 10,553 BTC leaving its wallets between January and September.

Looking closer at that list though, and it seemed to be pretty evident that they’re mostly miners.

Selling some of what is mined to pay the bills isn’t a new concept. Core Scientific actually got the best price of the group, at about $85,000 per coin. Sequans and KULR seemed to be the outliers here since they held BTC as a treasury asset.

According to data from Cryptoquant, newer BTC buyers may be hurting too. The short-term holder (STH) SOPR (7d average) had a reading of 0.99 at press time. Anything under 1 essentially means more people are selling at a loss than at a profit.

On 6th November, about 32,695 BTC held at a loss by STHs were sent to exchanges. That was roughly 89% of everything they moved there that day.

Then, on the 9th, BTC dropped to a new low near $74K. You’d expect more panic, but loss-making inflows fell to about 9,900 BTC.

The price fell lower, but fewer people rushed to dump. In past bull markets, a slowdown like that has sometimes come before a bounce.

At the time of writing, BTC was trading at around $73,686, with the same down by about 2.2% on the daily chart. In early October, the price was near $86K. This hinted at a 15% drop since!

Now, to its credit, Bitcoin did try to bounce.

On 4th November, Bitcoin’s price jumped back above $80K, but wiped it out the very next day.

The RSI was at 33.8, well below the Signal Line and not far from the oversold mark.

So, is a bounce on the way? Well, with fewer loss-making coins on exchanges, sellers are probably running low on steam.

#5147. Urgent Ethereum node patch issued due to hidden security flaws

Ethereum's Lighthouse urged all beacon node operators to install a high-priority security patch ahead of a planned vulnerability disclosure.

Ethereum consensus client Lighthouse released a security patch on Nov. 9 and urged operators of all its beacon nodes to upgrade as soon as possible.

The v8.3.3 release makes that work a high priority for users who stake and those who do not, but the release notice rates validator-client upgrades as low priority for staking users.

As a consensus client, Lighthouse connects with other clients in Ethereum's proof-of-stake network. Its beacon node works with an execution engine to validate transactions in blocks, while the validator client connects to the beacon node and manages keys, according to the Lighthouse Book.

Operators can also run a beacon node without a validator client. Lighthouse's documentation includes data analysis and applications among these non-staking uses, and those operators receive the same high-priority beacon-node instruction as staking users in the v8.3.3 update table.

The project's priority definitions put high-priority work on a timescale of hours or days, to be completed as soon as possible. Low-priority work belongs in the next routine update cycle, with two weeks given as an example.

The beacon-node upgrade is high priority with or without staking. Staking users have a separate, lower-priority validator-client update.

Upgrade the beacon node promptly. The validator-client update has low priority and belongs in the routine cycle.

Beacon nodes used for applications or data analysis have the same high-priority instruction. No validator-client priority applies to this group.

Staking and non-staking beacon nodes are high priority; staking validator clients can use the routine update cycle.

Vulnerability mechanics and potential impact remain undisclosed. High priority describes upgrade urgency. Hours or days and two weeks are illustrative category guidance, not fixed deadlines. No advisory publication date is given.

Map the release's current priority table to operator roles. Hours or days and the routine-cycle example come from Lighthouse's general definitions. Connectors show editorial sequence or component priorities, not network traffic; positions are not a time scale.

Vulnerability mechanics and potential impact remain undisclosed. High priority describes upgrade urgency. Hours or days and two weeks are illustrative category guidance, not fixed deadlines. No advisory publication date is given.

Maintainers say v8.3.3 introduces no breaking changes, but still direct users upgrading from v8.2.x or earlier to read the v8.3.0 release notes, an additional consideration for operators who have skipped intervening versions.

The release says technical details of the vulnerabilities will be disclosed later. Links to security advisories are due to be added once network operators have had time to upgrade.

That approach follows Sigma Prime's Nov. 5 explanation of its disclosure process. The Lighthouse developer says it initially holds back vulnerability information to give users time to update their nodes, then adds details to release notes and GitHub Security Advisories.

The v8.3.3 notice does not report active exploitation or identify losses, and attack mechanics and potential impact remain undisclosed. The high-priority label does not disclose the technical severity or consequences of an attack.

The request is specific to Lighthouse's beacon-node software. For operators running both Lighthouse components, completing a validator-client update alone would still leave the beacon-node instruction outstanding.

Checking which component is being upgraded is key because the two entries in the release table have different schedules. The withheld details also leave claims of theft or an imminent chain halt unsupported by this notice.

#5143. October CPI sparks another crypto wipeout, but is buying the Bitcoin dip too risky?

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Is the post-CPI FUD creating another opportunity to buy the fear?

Santiment analysts seem to think so. According to their report, retailers are becoming extremely bearish with only 0.82 bullish comments for every bearish comment on Bitcoin. However, this level of pessimism could signal a contrarian buying opportunity, as extreme retail fear has historically been seen near market bottoms.

The timing is no coincidence. Retail optimism has been fading as the U.S economy continues to deal with sticky inflation. U.S headline CPI was up 0.4% in October compared to expectations of 0.3% and core CPI increased by 0.3% versus expectations of 0.2%. The result? A shift in market expectations.

As can be seen in the chart above, expectations for rate hikes have been rising quickly. For instance, the chances of a 50 basis point increase in December have risen to 11%, while there is an expectation of a 25 basis point increase of 84%. This puts the Fed’s December decision back in focus.

And, the concerns do not stop there. Peter Schiff has also commented on the concern around sustained inflation. He noted how the CPI increased by 0.4% in October, taking the total increase in 2026 to 4.15%, with two months still left in the year. If the trend continues, the inflation could increase to 5% by the end of the year, adding further pressure on the Fed to keep monetary policy tight.

This means that Bitcoin [BTC] may be recording a hike in retail pessimism, with the same coinciding with increasingly bearish macro outlooks. This can be seen as a positive for Santiment’s contrarian indicator, but will the heightened macro risk mean that it is too risky to “buy the dip?”

The post-CPI reaction has triggered another crypto wipeout too.

Interestingly, there have been three instances of long liquidations above $500 million in under two weeks since November started. This alludes to huge waves of deleveraging in the market as traders get squeezed out of their longs. And yet, despite these leverage resets, there still seemed to be a prevalent bearish bias.

More importantly, on-chain data has been adding to the pressure. The supply of Tether has been shrinking at a much faster rate than when FTX collapsed.

Over the last 60 days, for instance, USDT’s market cap fell by $6.6 billion, more than double the amount it fell during December 2022. Meanwhile, as Bitcoin fell from $79,000 to $73,000 last week, large holders reduced their balances by more than 34,000 BTC, worth roughly $2.6 billion.

In essence, the market is not showing clear signs of contrarian buying just yet.

Instead, reduced liquidity and a lack of solid smart money accumulation suggested that this downtrend may not be indicative of the usual short-term to long-term holder transition phase. This would make retail pessimism a weaker bottom signal, especially as large holders continue to reduce their exposure.

Consequently, this puts Santiment’s contrarian indicator in question. Considering inflation worries, increasing December rate hike expectations, and weak on-chain indicators, the risk to reward on this Bitcoin dip could be unfavorable. Especially since the market could still be facing a deeper correction.

Rising retail fear could create a Bitcoin buying opportunity, but inflation and rate-hike concerns are adding pressure.

Falling liquidity, whale selling, and heavy long liquidations mean the market could face further downside.

#5141. Coinbase wins national trust charter, and strict OCC mandates apply

Coinbase's federal trust charter is effective, authorizing OCC-supervised crypto custody and a gradual transfer of client accounts.

Coinbase National Trust Company’s federal custody charter is now effective, moving the exchange’s institutional custody expansion beyond preliminary approval.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency’s (OCC) application register records Nov. 6 as the effective date. A final conditional approval letter dated Nov. 6 says the bank met its preopening requirements and authorizes it to open on Nov. 9.

That gives the new entity permission to provide cryptocurrency custody under federal fiduciary supervision. The OCC has also approved an arrangement to transfer accounts from Coinbase’s New York trust company over time.

Coinbase announced final approval on Nov. 9, saying the charter would bring a consistent federal framework to its custody business. The milestone follows the April 2 preliminary decision.

The OCC’s final approval permits cryptocurrency custody in a fiduciary capacity. That subjects the national trust company’s custody services to fiduciary duties and standards of behavior.

The letter also discloses a Sept. 1 agreement between Coinbase Custody Trust Company and the new national bank providing for a gradual transition of custody-service rights and responsibilities from the New York trust company to the national trust company.

The OCC approved the acquisition and assumption of those accounts and assets under an exemption from certain restrictions on transactions between banks and affiliates.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

The charter permits fiduciary custody. A separate agreement provides for a gradual account transfer.

OCC authorization brings fiduciary custody into the national trust company’s permitted scope.

The September 1 agreement provides for a gradual transfer from the New York trust company to the national trust company.

Individual account completion remains undisclosed.

The dates mark legal milestones, not a verified operating launch. The three-year migration horizon is the April plan.

Qualitative process diagram from the OCC register, April and final November letters, and Coinbase announcement. Dates label distinct legal milestones; timeline spacing is not proportional. Dashed account-transfer connector denotes a disclosed plan rather than a completed movement.

The dates mark legal milestones, not a verified operating launch. The three-year migration horizon is the April plan.

That gives the planned transition regulatory authorization. The final letter describes an intention to begin migration, while Coinbase’s Nov. 9 announcement supplies no completed-transfer figures or client-by-client schedule.

The April plan envisioned moving the entire custody business over the national bank’s three-year initial operating period.

The November conditions supersede those imposed in April, and they keep the bank within trust-company operations and related activities in its business plan.

During its first three operating years, significant deviations require 60 days’ prior notice and written OCC non-objection. The final letter specifically includes material changes to products and services and any offering of transactional services for custody-account customers.

The bank must also maintain at least $60 million in tier 1 capital, prescribed liquid-asset buffers and a separate reserve covering 180 days of operating expenses during that period.

The April decision described an uninsured institution, and the final approval preserves the limited trust-company scope.

This was a testnet demonstration using representative data, with no actual ratings published onchain or live dissemination processes involved.

Moody's Ratings and Chainlink completed a pilot demonstrating the cross-chain distribution of credit ratings across multiple blockchain networks using Chainlink's Cross-Chain Interoperability Protocol (CCIP).

The testnet pilot used Moody’s Token Integration Engine to simultaneously distribute credit insights across permissioned and permissionless networks, demonstrating how ratings information could be made available to tokenized assets across different blockchains while preserving Moody’s existing publication and governance processes.

Earlier this year, Moody's launched a token engine to bring its credit analysis onchain, starting with the Canton Network.

"The future of tokenized finance is unlikely to reside on a single blockchain, platform, or market infrastructure," said Fabian Astic, Global Head of Digital Economy at Moody's. "As digital markets continue to evolve, investors will increasingly expect access to credit ratings and associated information regardless of the underlying technology supporting an asset."

"This pilot explored how interoperable infrastructure can help make credit ratings available across multiple blockchain networks while preserving the governance and publication processes that support confidence in our analytical opinions," Astic said.

Between January 2017 and October 2026, Moody's Ratings rated or assessed more than 70 digital issuances, including digital bonds and tokenized funds.

Of note, Chainlink recently expanded its collaboration with S&P Global Ratings to bring vault risk assessments onchain.

#5137. 96% of older Bitcoin being sent to exchanges is now underwater

About 5,950 BTC reached exchanges below estimated acquisition cost on Nov. 10, accounting for 96% of that day's long-term-holder deposits.

Bitcoin's long-term holding cohort sent about 5,950 BTC to exchanges below estimated acquisition cost on Nov. 10. Underwater coins dominated this cohort's deposits, even as the volume arriving below cost fell from the previous day.

The loss-inflow series from analytics provider CoinGlass showed a 29.22% daily decline. Its total cohort inflows reached 6,182.67 BTC, including 232.72 BTC arriving above cost. Below-cost coins therefore accounted for about 96% of older-holder exchange deposits that day.

November 10, 2026: below-cost deposits fell 29.22% in a day but made up about 96% of the long-term cohort's exchange inflows.

Loss-making deposits dominated this cohort's exchange arrivals despite the daily decline.

Daily UTC CoinGlass inputs: loss 5,949.9482 BTC, profit 232.721 BTC, total 6,182.6693 BTC. Loss/total ×100 = 96.235912%, rounded to about 96%; bar uses the unrounded ratio. Displayed BTC rounds to two decimals. The 29.22% decline is provider-reported. Purpose branches encode no quantities.

CoinGlass defines the long-term cohort around a 155-day holding boundary. Its loss-inflow measure counts BTC sent to identified exchange addresses below estimated acquisition cost.

A separate profitability measure gives an earlier view of older-coin activity. CoinGlass reports a long-term-holder spent output profit ratio, or LTH-SOPR, of 0.82063 for Nov. 9, below the break-even level of 1.

The ratio compares the aggregate dollar value of older coins when spent with their value at creation. A reading below 1 means those spent coins moved at an aggregate loss. Unlike the deposit figures, this measure covers spending across the network.

Separate trading data also pointed to seller aggression. CryptoSlate reported on Nov. 10 that Glassnode's Nov. 9 snapshot showed higher spot turnover alongside negative spot cumulative volume delta. Negative spot cumulative volume delta means sell-initiated volume exceeded buy-initiated volume.

The next useful signals are whether below-cost deposit volume continues to fall and whether its share of cohort inflows declines. Nov. 10's smaller flow still carried a predominantly underwater mix, keeping potential supply pressure in focus.

This Bitcoin Developer’s Idea Would Make Quantum Attacks a Losing Bet

Bitcoin developer Cory Fields has an unusual idea for dealing with future quantum thieves: Make them risk their own Bitcoin every time they try to steal someone else’s.

In a November 4 post to the Bitcoin development mailing list, Fields outlined “quantum landmines” and two types of auctions designed to turn attacks on vulnerable wallets into expensive gambles. He called the ideas “thought experiments,” not a completed Bitcoin upgrade.

Bitcoin owners use a secret private key to authorize transactions. A matching public key lets the network check their signatures without learning the secret.

If the whole idea seems too hard to understand, we used AI to generate a video to help you grasp it:

Today’s computers cannot realistically calculate that private key from the public one. A sufficiently powerful quantum computer could use a mathematical technique called Shor’s algorithm to do it, potentially letting a thief spend coins as if they owned them.

Some older Bitcoin outputs have exposed public keys, and certain newer formats reveal them too. Other addresses hide the key until someone spends, so the risk is not identical for every wallet.

Researchers call the hypothetical arrival of a computer capable of these attacks “Q-Day.” No publicly demonstrated machine can steal Bitcoin this way today, and nobody knows exactly when one might exist.

Imagine someone owns 1 BTC in an old, potentially vulnerable wallet. Before Q-Day, this person creates a tiny, separate quantum-safe Bitcoin output containing a hidden proof that they controlled the original private key while quantum theft was still impossible.

Think of it as a sealed ownership receipt. Outsiders can see the small output, but not the evidence tucked inside it, or even that it is a trap.

Now imagine a future thief uses a quantum computer to recover the user’s old private key. Under Fields’s suggested rules, the thief cannot simply take her 1 BTC: They must add 1 BTC of their own from a quantum-safe wallet as collateral.

Both coins enter a restricted output worth 2 BTC. The thief must wait through a challenge period—30 days in Fields’s example—before spending it freely.

The wallet owner notices the transaction and reveals the pre-Q-Day proof. The network then allows the owner to move the full 2 BTC to the quantum-safe address they committed to earlier: their original coin, plus the thief’s collateral.

The attacker has no way to know in advance which old wallets contain these hidden receipts. Even a successful quantum key recovery could become a 1 BTC loss.

The wallet owner would also need matching collateral to initiate a normal post-Q-Day move of her own legacy coin. If they have no spare BTC, the same rule intended to hurt thieves could make moving her savings difficult.

Landmines only work when an owner prepares one before Q-Day and reveals it in time. They cannot protect coins whose keys are already lost, including some of the early Bitcoin holdings widely believed to be inaccessible.

Fields proposes a second mechanism called a staked auction. Before Q-Day, someone could lock up quantum-safe Bitcoin and secretly register a bid against a specific old wallet they expect thieves to target.

Suppose an apparently abandoned wallet holds 50 BTC. A future attacker tries to move it and posts another 50 BTC as collateral; during the auction period, someone who committed a bid in advance can challenge the attempted theft.

In Fields’s example, a successful challenger claims part of the attacker’s collateral while the original vulnerable coins are destroyed rather than awarded to the bidder. The point is to deprive thieves of a reliable payday, not return the coins to a missing owner.

His third idea, a sats auction, requires no advance stake. Instead, a vulnerable-coin spend would trigger a contest in which the highest bidder gets the coins minus their bid, while the runner-up pays their bid and gets nothing.

That resembles a notorious auction game where two bidders keep raising their offers because neither wants to be the person who loses money for nothing. A thief might avoid starting a contest that could cost more than the coins they hoped to steal.

One proposed response to quantum risk is to restrict spending from outdated wallets after a migration deadline. That might prevent theft, but could also permanently lock out legitimate owners who never moved their coins.

Fields is exploring a different trade-off: Keep old coins potentially spendable, but make attempted transfers costly and open to challenges. Bitcoin cannot tell an honest owner from a quantum thief if both can produce the same valid signature.

The trade-off is severe, considering that honest owners might need large collateral deposits, inactive holders could miss their chance to object, and auction rules might burn coins belonging to people who are still alive and simply offline.

Bitcoin would first need a quantum-safe way to hold and spend funds. Wallets would then need to support hidden ownership commitments, while Bitcoin’s consensus rules would have to enforce collateral, waiting periods, special recovery transactions, and auctions.

Developers would also need to agree on when the new rules activate, how much collateral is required, and what happens to losing bids or leftover funds. Fields believes some mechanics could be introduced through a soft fork, a type of Bitcoin rule change, but has not supplied the detailed design.

None of these protections exists in Bitcoin today. Fields has published no implementation or activation schedule, and his original post leaves the auction payouts and even the desired outcome of an auction unresolved.

#5134. MEGA commits $30 million to new products, starting with AI inference

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The MegaETH Foundation rebrands as MEGA and commits $30 million to new products, with an AI inference market set to launch in December.

The MegaETH Foundation, the team behind the Ethereum Layer 2 network MegaETH, has rebranded as MEGA and committed $30 million to new products, starting with an AI inference market planned for December.

The announcement comes after months of work in stealth mode, MEGA said Tuesday, adding that the team will now also develop new products alongside the MegaETH network.

All new products will run on MegaETH, MEGA said. Planned network upgrades, including fast finality, will also help support its AI inference product.

Inference is the process of running a trained AI model to produce an output. MEGA said providers charge different prices for similar services, but buyers may find it hard to know the risks of using cheaper providers they are not familiar with.

"There are still huge gaps between what providers charge for comparable inference," MegaETH co-founder Yilong Li said in a statement. "We think those gaps can be dramatically reduced."

MEGA calls its approach "Purified Intelligence," aiming to make inference from different providers more interchangeable, allowing more suppliers to compete in a global market.

Asked how the market would work and which providers or models would be available, MegaETH co-founder Shuyao Kong told The Block that MEGA had intentionally held back those details until the December launch.

"We believe crypto is the only technology that makes AI fair and open," she said, adding that developers will be the target customers for the inference market.

The $30 million will come from MEGA's existing treasury to fund a range of products, Kong said, noting inference as the project's "largest move."

MEGA said its mandate includes expanding the uses of the MEGA token. When asked what role the token would have in the inference market, Kong said: "This is our mandate, so wherever there are ways to utilize the MEGA token, we will."

The MegaETH team has raised more than $80 million to date across venture funding, community rounds and token sales. That includes a $20 million seed round announced in June 2024, led by Dragonfly with backing from Vitalik Buterin, Joseph Lubin and others; a $10 million Echo round in December 2024; about $13 million from its Fluffle NFT sale in February 2025; and about $40 million from its public token sale in October 2025, according to Kong. She said the public sale amount reflects discounts for buyers who agreed to lock their tokens for one year.

Kong also noted that MegaETH bought back some investors' stakes last year. As The Block previously reported, the team repurchased a 4.75% stake comprising equity and token warrants from pre-seed investors in summer 2025.

The MegaETH network launched its public mainnet earlier this year and currently has about $12 million in total value locked, down from its peak of over $245 million, according to DefiLlama data.

The MEGA token went live in April this year and is currently trading at around $0.05, down over 76% from its all-time high, according to The Block's MEGA price page.

#5133. US card debt hits $1.29 trillion as Bitcoin loans expose a collateral divide

US card debt reached $1.29 trillion. Bitcoin-backed loans advertise lower rates, but borrowers must weigh fees and the risk of an automatic collateral sale.

US credit-card balances reached $1.29 trillion in the third quarter, the New York Fed reported on Nov. 10. Bitcoin-backed loans advertise lower borrowing rates, but the comparison comes with a different risk: losing the collateral in an automatic sale.

The New York Fed's report puts card balances $22 billion higher than the previous quarter and $52 billion higher than a year earlier.

Separately, the Federal Reserve's latest measure of interest assessed on card accounts was 22.36%, while Coinbase advertises crypto-backed borrowing from 5.1%.

That gap can translate into substantially lower modeled interest costs, but accessing it requires assets. A $10,000 payout would require $25,500 in Bitcoin at a chosen 40% initial loan-to-value ratio once the processing fee is financed.

The rate may be attractive, but the collateral can be sold automatically if the loan becomes too large relative to its backing.

Consider a constant $10,000 card balance for one year, with no principal repayments and simple interest at the Fed's 22.36% measure, and the modeled interest cost is $2,236.

For Coinbase's variable-rate product, assume a payout worth $10,000 in USDC and hold the advertised 5.1% rate constant for a year. Coinbase's variable-loan processing fee is 2% on the first $250,000, with 1% charged on amounts above that tier.

The $200 fee brings the opening debt to $10,200, and simple interest on that amount is $520.20. Adding the fee produces a modeled first-year borrowing cost of $720.20.

The gross difference is about $1,516. This simplified illustration gives neither a Bitcoin borrower quote nor guaranteed savings, and it does not calculate a full APR. It excludes platform fees, compounding, rate changes, conversion costs, and liquidation effects.

Coinbase says a platform fee may apply monthly to variable-rate loans, and the lending rate also changes with supply and demand, so 5.1% cannot be treated as a promised yearlong cost. The actual offer determines how much of the apparent gap survives.

On the card side, the 22.36% figure in the Federal Reserve's Nov. 6 consumer-credit release appears in the August and third-quarter observations for commercial-bank accounts assessed interest. The corresponding figure for all accounts was 21.19%.

The Fed annualizes finance charges relative to the average daily balances on which those charges were imposed, excluding accounts without finance charges. The rate cannot simply be applied to every dollar of the New York Fed's $1.29 trillion estimate.

Coinbase says eligible, verified US customers outside New York can borrow without a credit check. Borrowing capacity depends on eligible collateral, with limits shown in the product. Removing the credit check replaces it with an asset requirement.

Through the integration, pledged Bitcoin is converted into Coinbase Wrapped Bitcoin (cbBTC) and transferred to a smart contract on Morpho, a lending protocol on Base.

Collateral held there is marked locked and nontradable, although qualifying excess collateral can be withdrawn within loan-to-value (LTV) limits. Variable-rate loans have no scheduled minimum payments or fixed due date, but interest continues accruing. Payment flexibility still requires monitoring the collateral.

LTV divides outstanding debt by the collateral's current market value, so a $10,000 debt at an illustrative 40% initial LTV needs $25,000 of Bitcoin before fees.

Including the financed $200 processing fee raises that requirement to $25,500 to preserve the same starting ratio.

If debt reaches the market's liquidation threshold relative to collateral, a sale can happen automatically. For Bitcoin-backed borrowing, Coinbase describes repayment of debt and interest with an additional 4.38% penalty. Any Bitcoin left after the required liquidation returns to the Coinbase account.

For a hypothetical Bitcoin-backed loan with an 86% liquidation threshold and constant debt, a loan beginning at 40% LTV reaches that threshold after a roughly 53.5% fall in collateral value. A separate loan beginning at 60% LTV reaches the same threshold after about a 30.2% fall.

Illustrative $10,000 USDC payout: the 2% financed fee makes debt $10,200. At a chosen 40% initial LTV, the Bitcoin pledge is $25,500.

$10,200 debt backed by $25,500 in Bitcoin. With an assumed 86% threshold and constant debt, a 53.5% fall reaches liquidation.

The same $10,200 debt starts against $17,000 in Bitcoin. With an assumed 86% threshold and constant debt, a 30.2% fall reaches liquidation.

A higher starting LTV needs less collateral but leaves less room for Bitcoin to fall before liquidation.

Price fall=1−initial LTV/.86: 53.5% or 30.2%, rounded to 1 decimal. Bar widths share a $25,500 scale; debt and bar heights stay fixed.

A larger cushion requires more collateral or less borrowing. Coinbase also identifies protocol security, liquidity, and Coinbase Smart Wallet issues as risks, adding dependencies alongside the obligation to repay.

The New York Fed said credit-card transitions into early and serious delinquency improved slightly in the third quarter. Annualized flows into serious delinquency were 6.9%, versus 7.1% a year earlier.

In a separate Nov. 10 analysis, New York Fed economists said card delinquency increased most sharply after 2022 among borrowers in lower-income neighborhoods, widening the gap with higher-income areas.

For someone with sufficient eligible assets, crypto-backed borrowing may reduce interest costs after fees. For someone without them, the advertised rate does not resolve the financing problem, as borrowing capacity hinges on the assets available to pledge.

The useful comparison is the fee-inclusive offer against the amount of crypto committed and the liquidation buffer left behind. A lower borrowing rate can coexist with a new risk of losing Bitcoin through an automatic sale when the borrower intended to keep it.

Cryptocurrency and derivatives gains helped the company report an $8 million quarterly profit.

Bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) mining hardware maker Canaan Canaan Inc. (CAN) sold 1 million TH/s of computing power in the third quarter, bringing in $4.8 million from mining equipment, down 96% from $118.6 million in the same period last year.

Canaan's overall revenue fell 90% to $14.5 million from $150.5 million a year earlier, according to its financial results published Tuesday. Canaan attributed the drop in hardware revenue to lower computing power sold and weaker average selling prices amid reduced market demand.

When Canaan reported its third-quarter 2025 results last November, it had sold more than 10 EH/s of mining machines and produced 267 BTC, The Block reported at the time. The company mined 133 BTC in the latest quarter, generating mining revenue of $9.5 million, compared to $30.6 million in Q3 2025.

Nevertheless, Canaan posted $8 million in net income for Q3 2026, compared with a $27.7 million loss a year earlier amid a $20.1 million fair-value gain on cryptocurrency holdings and another $31.9 million on financial derivatives. However, its operating loss widened to $42.9 million from $23.9 million.

Canaan Chief Financial Officer Jin "James" Cheng attributed the gains to bitcoin's higher price at the end of September. "We recognize that this non-cash gain is distinct from underlying operating performance," he said in the release.

Earlier this year, Canaan acquired Cipher Mining's 49% stake in three West Texas bitcoin mining projects for approximately $40 million. The three projects had a combined installed hashrate of 4.87 EH/s at the end of September, according to the firm.

ERCOT classified Canaan's proposed 1 GW Duval County power project as "Studied Load – Firm" on a conditional basis, and further studies and approvals are still pending. Its second 1 GW Texas project, in Zapata County, remains in early development, the firm said.

Of the approximately 1,875 BTC Canaan held at the end of September, 1,258 BTC was pledged for secured loans. The company also announced a $20 million share buyback program under a $100 million authorization approved by its board on Nov. 6.

#5129. Hyperscale Data (GPUS) Sells Its Last Bitcoin for AI Data Center, Months After Chasing $100 Million Treasury

Hyperscale Data sold its remaining 211.56 bitcoin for about $16 million by Nov. 8, bringing sales since late July to about 1,113 BTC as it races to energize 10 MW of AI capacity in Michigan in December.

Hyperscale Data has sold the last of its bitcoin, the NYSE American-listed company said Tuesday, unloading about 211.56 BTC for roughly $16 million to pay down debt and fund an AI data center in Michigan.

The sales were completed by Nov. 8 at about $76,000 per coin. Since it first sold part of its reserve in late July, Hyperscale has sold approximately 1,113 bitcoin for about $74.4 million, the company said.

That works out to an average of roughly $66,800 per coin. At today’s price near $74,200, the same 1,113 BTC would be worth about $82.6 million.

The company, which trades under the ticker GPUS, said the money will go toward its Michigan site, where it aims to energize the first 10 megawatts of critical IT capacity in December.

“We believe bringing that capacity online is our quickest path to profitability,” CEO Will Horne said in the release. “Selling our Bitcoin reserves reduces our exposure to Bitcoin price swings and gives us cash to pay down debt and fund the work in Michigan. We believe that’s the best use of this capital for all our stockholders.”

The exit is a sharp reversal from Hyperscale’s plans this summer. In late July, the company reported holding more than 1,106 bitcoin and said it wanted to build a $100 million digital asset treasury and reach full parity between its bitcoin holdings and its market capitalization.

“Every Bitcoin we acquire further strengthens Hyperscale Data’s balance sheet and expands our financial flexibility,” Executive Chairman Milton “Todd” Ault III said at the time. “We intend to continue building our Bitcoin position over time.”

A week later, Hyperscale disclosed its first sale, about 150.5 BTC, leaving it with roughly 958.5 BTC as of Aug. 2, even as its Ault Capital Group subsidiary bought about 15 BTC on the open market. The holdings were split between that unit and Sentinum. Ault said then that the company planned to keep a long-term position while tapping it for short-term flexibility, adding, “We are confident in our ability to use Bitcoin as pristine collateral.”

Tuesday’s release closes that chapter. Hyperscale said it still mines bitcoin at its Montana site and expects any bitcoin it holds on its balance sheet going forward to come “primarily” from its own mining operations.

Hyperscale is the latest public company to give up a bitcoin treasury in favor of data center spending. Keel sold its entire bitcoin treasury for $192 million in the third quarter, and Riot and Hut 8 sold thousands of bitcoin to fund AI buildouts and buybacks.

Larger miners are moving the same way. MARA said Monday it sold 13,597 BTC for about $1.1 billion after Sept. 30 and plans to keep selling to fund AI infrastructure, convertible note puts and share repurchases.

Hyperscale’s structure is more complicated than a pure-play miner’s. Its Sentinum subsidiary runs the data center business, while Ault Capital Group, a hybrid private equity firm and operating company, holds a mix of lending, defense, industrial and hotel businesses. Hyperscale expects to divest Ault Capital Group in 2027 and become a data center owner and operator.

The company said it expects to file its third-quarter 10-Q on or before Nov. 23. Because of a newly proposed exchange offer for its Class A common stock, it is also moving its virtual Investor Day from Nov. 12 to Nov. 23, when management plans to update investors on debt reduction and the December energization target.

Hyperscale did not say how much debt the bitcoin proceeds have retired so far or how much remains outstanding.

#5128. Tokenized stock trading hits $2.7B even though trades can cost 3% more

Modeled $10,000 trades exposed wide cost differences between stock tokens, even when their quoted prices stayed close to the underlying shares.

Tokenized stocks recorded about $3 billion in decentralized-exchange transactions over seven days, according to figures reported on Nov. 4.

US stocks rallied that day as Republicans lost unified control of Washington, with the S&P 500 up 1.6%, the Dow up about 3% and the Nasdaq up 1.4%.

A modeled $10,000 round trip in tokenized Coinbase shares carried a quote gap near $303 that week, about 3% of the trade.

Fillable's Nov. 3 to Nov. 9 study of Solana tokenized stocks quoted buys and sells every 15 minutes during regular US hours, using recent IEX trades as the reference price.

It accounted for pool fees and price slippage, and the figures model quote gaps from simulated trades. An S&P 500 ETF token (SPYx) carried a gap of $20.60, or 0.21% of a $10,000 trade.

Tesla's TSLAx came in at $43.60, Nvidia's NVDAx at $44.30, and Apple's AAPLx at $88.80. Coinbase's COINx reached $303, Robinhood's HOODx $371, and Palantir's PLTRx $699.

Selected Solana stock tokens during regular US hours on Nov. 3-9. Quotes were simulated every 15 minutes against recent IEX trades, pool fees and price impact are included.

Source: Fillable — Solana tokenized stock prices, Nov. 3-9

COINx's gap is about 14.7 times SPYx's, and PLTRx's is about 34 times. COINx carried a median buy premium near 153 basis points and a sale discount near 149.

In an illustration with those medians, $10,000 in USDC buys about $9,849 of exposure at the reference price, and an immediate reversal returns about $9,703.

Fillable measured 22 stocks, and 19 had a midpoint within 0.1% of the underlying share price at a $1,000 trade size.

A midpoint reflects where a token is marked, and a buyer moving through a pool receives a price shaped by available liquidity, the pool's curve, and the trade size. The study excludes network fees, some token-to-token conversions, and the savings from splitting an order across pools, so it covers less than an all-in wallet-to-wallet cost.

Coin Metrics' Nov. 3 State of the Network found tokenized Nvidia order-book depth within 1% of price down 19% on average when US markets were closed on Bybit and MEXC. On Hyperliquid, order-book depth for the same token fell about 33%.

Tokenized Nvidia prices showed weak correlations of 0.24 and 0.30 with the next US open in the evening and overnight windows, and alignment improved as the open approached. Fillable's Nov. 9 index shows a median $17.90 round-trip quote cost across ten major stocks and funds, using each asset's cheapest pool across four chains.

The median was $22.70 during regular US market hours and $15.80 when US markets were closed. Unlike the venue-specific Nvidia order books, this index selects each asset’s cheapest eligible pool, so the two studies do not measure the same markets.

Brokerages already offer extended-hours trading in eligible securities, so the tokenized edge is wallet access and crypto-native settlement, subject to issuer and jurisdictional limits.

Medians for simulated $10,000 round trips across ten fixed stocks and funds, each using its cheapest eligible pool across Solana, Robinhood Chain, Base and BNB Chain on Nov. 9. Fees and price impact are included, network fees excluded.

Source: Fillable 10 — Nov. 9 index and session medians

Bitquery's October study counted $10 billion of tokenized-stock DEX turnover across six issuers and five chains. For Oct. 2–31, 65% of turnover occurred outside regular US hours, and the 100 busiest wallets produced 64% of Coinbase-issued token volume.

About 10% of Robinhood-issued token volume from Oct. 2–31 came from transactions that bought and sold the same token within one transaction, consistent with automated arbitrage, against about 2% for Coinbase-issued tokens.

Adjusting for those round trips cuts Robinhood's monthly lead over Coinbase from $119 million to about $11 million.

NYSE-backed OKXICE faced objections covering 57 of its 63 planned stock tickers. Meanwhile, Dune data showed a median of $92 in holdings per decentralized equity liquidity pool as of Aug. 31.

Of 5,484 pools, 78 held about 81% of measured assets. The $92 is a pool-holdings median, a gauge of capital concentration and separate from execution quality at any venue.

The SEC has said tokenized securities can carry materially different rights depending on structure, and its September Innovation Exemption sets conditions for limited experiments. A token tracking a stock can differ from the stock in ownership, voting, dividend, and redemption rights.

If higher volume attracts market makers and more liquidity becomes available for $10,000 orders, quote gaps could narrow across major tokens, including in off-hours sessions.

The measures to watch are the share of $10,000 orders executable within 50 basis points of the underlying stock, depth within 1% of the reference price in and out of regular hours, and wallet concentration.

If activity proves temporary or remains concentrated in arbitrage, liquidity providers could withdraw capital and costs could rise even while the market stays open around the clock. In a trading halt or redemption disruption, a token could carry a theoretical price while holders face exits at unacceptable prices.

A market whose turnover doubles with spreads and depth unchanged has grown busier, and one whose spreads narrow and depth rises has improved the service investors receive.

Execution quality, the cash recovered on a sale, and the rights attached to the token will decide whether 24/7 access is worth its price.

We just issued a press release from our board of directors. Read the release: https://t.co/W9yXWJzbkk

— NVIDIA Newsroom (@nvidianewsroom) November 8, 2026

The investigation follows a Financial Times report on Saturday that a U.S. government memo, written earlier this year based on intelligence information, said the Nvidia CEO had been romantically involved with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed, citing people familiar with the memo. U.S. intelligence believes she was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, the FT reported. Nvidia declined to comment to the newspaper on the memo. Huang's email to staff, sent on Sunday, did not name the person with whom he had an affair.

Lawmakers from both parties are seeking answers. Republican leaders have asked Huang to appear privately before the House China, foreign affairs and intelligence committees, according to the FT, while Sen. Chris Coons (D-DE), who will chair the Senate Foreign Relations Committee from January, pledged in a tweet that "Congress will investigate and get answers."

The FT's report built on a New York Times investigation last month, which said U.S. intelligence agencies had concluded that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese citizen, was a Chinese intelligence asset, and that surveillance of her had revealed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. President Donald Trump was briefed on the findings roughly a year ago and chose not to act on them, according to the Times.

U.S. officials suspected Megaspeed of helping Chinese companies get around restrictions on advanced AI chips, and the Commerce Department's investigation into the company has been handed to the Justice Department, the Times reported. Megaspeed's sister company in Malaysia bought at least $4.8 billion worth of AI equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026, according to trade records cited by the newspaper.

Nvidia told the Times that Huang's interactions with Ms. Huang were "not unusual or unexpected," and that customers like Megaspeed receive "ordinary business information." Megaspeed said it had retained outside counsel to conduct an internal investigation, Ms. Huang did not respond to the newspaper's requests for comment, and China's embassy in Washington dismissed the allegations as "groundless smears and slanders."

In an email to employees on Sunday, Huang apologized to his family and colleagues. "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did," he wrote, according to a copy published by CNBC.

"Today's news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption," the company told CNBC.

Nvidia shares were down 5% at $177.32 in premarket trading early on Monday, after closing at $186.64 on Friday, according to Yahoo Finance.

#5121. MARA Sells 13,597 Bitcoin for $1.1 Billion, Says More Sales Are Coming

MARA sold about 40% of its bitcoin stack after Sept. 30, used $750 million to repay all its BTC-backed term loans and said it will keep selling to fund AI infrastructure, convertible note puts and buybacks.

MARA Holdings sold 13,597 bitcoin for about $1.1 billion after the third quarter ended and used $750 million of the cash to pay off all of its bitcoin-backed term loans, the miner said Monday in its Q3 shareholder letter.

The coins went for roughly $81,039 each. MARA held 34,012 BTC on Sept. 30, so the sale cut about 40% of the stack in a matter of weeks.

Repaying the loans returned 17,477 bitcoin that had been pledged as collateral, leaving less than 5% of MARA’s holdings loaned or pledged, the company said. Subtracting the sale from the quarter-end figure implies about 20,400 BTC left, before counting coins mined since.

The letter makes clear the selling is not over. “We intend to continue using bitcoin to build cash for purposes such as AI infrastructure opportunities, to satisfy the puts on our convertible notes that become exercisable next year, and potential share repurchases,” MARA wrote.

The board also authorized a buyback of up to $500 million of common stock after quarter-end.

MARA spent years building one of the largest bitcoin stacks among public companies. The shift away from holding came in stages. The company said it began permitting sales of mined bitcoin in 2025 and in 2026 expanded the policy to cover bitcoin already on its balance sheet.

It sold about 26,984 bitcoin for $1.9 billion in the first nine months of the year, including 3,891 BTC in the third quarter at an average of $75,300. It mined 2,247 BTC in the quarter and bought none.

Year to date, MARA has cut total debt by $1.4 billion, or 37%. It ended September with $946.5 million in cash and about $3.8 billion in cash and bitcoin combined, plus 1,408 BTC lent out that earned about $2.5 million in interest during the quarter.

MARA’s post-quarter sale fetched about $6,800 more per coin than bitcoin’s price near $74,200 on Tuesday morning.

The quarter’s headline profit came from the coins, not the mines. Revenue fell 35% to $164.2 million from $252.4 million a year earlier, even as energized hashrate rose 18% to 71.2 EH/s.

Net income rose to $632.1 million, or $1.28 a diluted share, from $123.1 million, helped by an $885.3 million gain on the fair value of digital assets.

Mining itself got slightly more expensive. Purchased energy cost per bitcoin at MARA’s owned sites was $39,674, up from $39,235 a year earlier, while blocks won rose 2% to 644.

“Bitcoin built the foundation. Power created the opportunity,” the letter opens, describing a strategy to “maximize the value of every megawatt” MARA controls.

MARA said it is targeting two data center leases before year-end but warned that “market conditions are fluid and that timing could slip into next year.” It received FERC approval for its Long Ridge natural gas plant purchase, currently authorized to sell 485 MW, and expects to close in the coming weeks. It also secured rights to develop a Matagorda County, Texas site with up to 2 GW of power capacity, and its Exaion unit signed a four-year, $79 million GPU-as-a-service contract with its first U.S. customer.

The move puts MARA in step with peers pulling away from bitcoin. Riot and Hut 8 sold thousands of bitcoin to fund AI projects and buybacks, Keel sold its entire treasury, and Core Scientific plans to exit mining by year-end.

MARA still describes bitcoin mining as its operating foundation, one that keeps sites earning revenue while higher-value infrastructure is built out. With roughly 13,600 fewer coins on the books and a stated plan to keep selling, the miner that once carried one of the largest corporate stacks is now using that stack to pay for its next business.

#5120. Bitcoin holds $73,000 as odds of a December 50 bps rate hike jump

Hot inflation lifted bets on a bigger December Fed hike, but even a quarter-point increase could pressure Bitcoin if officials signal higher rates for longer.

The odds of a 50-basis-point Federal Reserve hike in December rose from 0% to 13.6% on Nov. 10 after October CPI beat forecasts, as Bitcoin fell to an intraday low below $73,000.

Meanwhile, the odds of a 25-basis-point hike climbed from 84% to 86.4%, according to a Nov. 10 CME FedWatch snapshot reported by Barron's.

Headline CPI rose 0.4% versus a 0.3% forecast, and core rose 0.3% versus 0.2%, meeting the condition Governor Christopher Waller set for considering a 50 bps move.

The market is pricing more tightening, with 25 bps the dominant outcome. The no-hike probability dropped from 16% to 0%, so the 25 bps odds rose alongside the 50 bps odds.

Weighting the three outcomes, the expected December hike moved from 21.0 bps to 28.4 bps, up 7.4 bps. A 50/50 split between the two sizes would imply 37.5 bps, so the market sits closer to its old expectation than to a 50 bps base case.

The odds ratio favoring 50 over 25 would have to rise more than sixfold before 50 bps became the likelier size.

Dec. 9 decision probabilities from the CME FedWatch snapshot quoted in the supplied article and attributed there to Barron's. Each bar totals 100%.

Source: CME FedWatch — historical snapshot quoted in supplied article

October's report was hotter than forecast and cooler than September on the headline, which slowed from 0.6% to 0.4%. Core stayed at 0.3% for a third month, and transportation services rose 0.8%.

At a constant 0.3% a month, core inflation compounds to about 3.7% annualized, a run-rate calculation that stands apart from an official annual figure. The BLS omitted an annual October comparison, since the 2025 government shutdown interrupted the underlying data collection.

Waller's threshold opens consideration of a 50 bps hike, and committee backing is a separate matter. The Fed held at 3.75% to 4% on Oct. 28 by a 10-2 vote, and both dissenters wanted 25 bps.

Seasonally adjusted CPI-U changes from the preceding month, as reported in the Nov. 10 release. Core excludes food and energy. Month labels refer to the measured month. BLS omitted most October year-over-year comparisons because October 2025 survey data were unavailable.

Source: BLS — October 2026 CPI release, Table A, retrieved Nov. 10

Three developments could strengthen the case for 50 bps at the FOMC’s December meeting and shape Bitcoin's outlook.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

October core PCE on Nov. 25 would need to confirm CPI, with monthly readings near 0.3% to 0.4% and broad price strength, against September's 0.3% monthly and 3.1% annual core PCE gain.

The Dec. 4 jobs report would need to show a labor market that can absorb more tightening. October payrolls rose 165,000 against a 12-month average of 48,000, unemployment was 4.1%, and hourly earnings rose 0.4%.

Several voting members would also need to back faster tightening publicly, and oil and sticky services costs would need to persist.

PPI arrives Nov. 13, the minutes of the October meeting Nov. 18, and the Fed's communications blackout begins Nov. 28, before the Dec. 4 jobs report.

The decision comes Dec. 9, and November CPI lands Dec. 10, one day after the Fed's decision, so officials decide before the next CPI print arrives. Softer PCE or hiring could weaken the case for a half-point increase.

A Reuters poll of 101 economists on Nov. 6 to 10 expects 25 bps in December, to 4.00%-4.25%. Of those, 56 see December as the final hike, while 45 expect at least two further increases in total, including December.

Even a 25 bps move could lift yields and tighten financial conditions if the Fed signals more increases in 2027 than markets expect. For Bitcoin, the risk is not just December's hike size, but a shift toward higher rates for longer. Cross-market moves on Nov. 10 illustrated that pressure.

The two-year Treasury yield rose about 19 bps to 4.74%, the 10-year neared 4.99%, the dollar index gained 0.6%, and gold fell more than 2%.

Farside Investors shows US spot Bitcoin ETF net outflows of about $1.5 billion from Nov. 2 to Nov. 9.

Glassnode's Nov. 4 report found about 38% of short-term holder supply in profit, though much of the leverage built since August had cleared and spot volume ran about 1.5 times its pre-rally level.

The leverage reset may reduce the risk of another forced-selling cascade, but it does not rule out further sharp losses.

Daily net flows across US spot Bitcoin ETFs. Trading sessions from Nov. 2-Nov. 9 sum to negative $1.5 billion.

Source: Farside Investors — Bitcoin ETF daily total net flows

In its Nov. 4 report, the firm identified a modeled long-liquidation band at $73,000 to $76,000. These are estimated levels where leveraged positions could be forced to close, not confirmed buying support.

Measured from $73,000, a move to $70,000 would represent a further 4.1% decline; the round number alone does not establish technical support.

Glassnode also identified $60,000 to $63,000, 17.8% to 13.7% below, as a concentration of modeled Bitcoin long liquidations left by a breakout. That liquidation estimate is not a price forecast or a worst-case floor, and the report does not tie it to a particular Fed decision.

If core PCE cools toward 0.2% month over month, hiring slows, and officials favor quarter-point steps, a 25 bps December increase with a softer outlook would become more plausible. Bitcoin could then recover toward the $75,700 to $77,700 cost-basis levels in Glassnode's Nov. 4 report, provided ETF selling eases.

If inflation stays sticky and employment holds up, a quarter-point increase accompanied by signals of further tightening in 2027 could keep pressure on Bitcoin. The precise downside would also depend on ETF flows, spot demand and leverage.

Continued ETF outflows, weak spot demand and forced selling could deepen a decline, especially if markets price in more aggressive tightening. But neither the liquidation map nor the Fed outlook establishes that Bitcoin will reach $60,000 to $63,000.

The readings to watch are PCE on Nov. 25, jobs on Dec. 4, and the tone of the Fed before its blackout.

#5119. Trump Says He Knows 'Nothing' About World Liberty Financial as He Defends UAE Ties

Trump Says He Knows 'Nothing' About World Liberty Financial as He Defends UAE Ties

U.S. President Donald Trump has defended his family's stake in crypto venture World Liberty Financial, saying he knows "nothing" about the firm despite being a co-owner, in an interview after last week's midterm elections.

Asked by columnist Ross Douthat why his co-ownership of a company partly owned by investors linked to the United Arab Emirates government was different from the kind of arrangement he would call corrupt if it involved the Biden family, Trump replied: "Here's the difference [... ] I'm gonna tell you why. Because I know nothing about it," according to a transcript published by CBS News.

Pressed on why he did not simply divest, Trump said most of his money is managed by Wall Street firms through index funds, and that his sons run the family business. "It's hard to say to them, 'Don't do anything anymore for four years because I'm president,'" he said.

When Douthat asked whether foreign investors in the company believe they are buying influence, Trump said: "I don't know." He argued that conflicts of interest have dogged presidents "going back to George Washington," adding that past presidents "own something, whatever crypto was at the time."

"There's crypto, and before that there was oil," Trump said, adding that, "every president has had this problem."

"I'm a bigger name than other presidents, whether we like it or not," Trump said.

World Liberty Financial, which Eric Trump announced in August 2024, issues the WLFI governance token and the USD1 stablecoin. In January, it launched World Liberty Markets, a lending and borrowing platform built on DeFi protocol Dolomite.

Its UAE links have drawn scrutiny from Democrats. Aryam Investment, a UAE-backed entity tied to the country's national security adviser, Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed, agreed to buy a 49% stake in World Liberty Financial for $500 million four days before Trump's January 2025 inauguration, Decrypt reported in February, citing The Wall Street Journal. The deal, signed by Eric Trump on World Liberty's behalf, reportedly preceded the administration's reversal of restrictions on advanced AI chip sales to the UAE. A World Liberty spokesperson said at the time that neither Trump nor his Middle East envoy, Steve Witkoff, had "any involvement whatsoever" in the transaction, ABC News reported. Sen. Chris Murphy (D-CT) described the arrangement in February as "potentially criminal conduct." Trump has previously said he was not aware of the deal.

The company's UAE ties have also surfaced in its legal battle with Tron founder Justin Sun. Sun's lawyers asked a federal court to sanction World Liberty, alleging the firm delayed disclosing UAE ownership that could defeat federal jurisdiction over his lawsuit. World Liberty has called Sun's legal campaign a "meritless PR stunt."

The Trump family's financial stake in the venture is set out in World Liberty's own disclosures. DT Marks DEFI LLC, an entity affiliated with Trump and certain family members, owns about 38% of the holding company behind World Liberty Financial, holds 22.5 billion WLFI tokens, and is entitled to 75% of the net proceeds from WLFI token sales, according to the company. A separate Trump-affiliated entity has an indirect claim on interest earned on the reserves backing USD1. The disclosures state that no member of the Trump family is an officer, director or employee of World Liberty, though Trump's sons have remained involved with the company, Decrypt reported earlier this year.

#5115. Coinbase Joins Circle, Ripple With Final OCC Approval for Federal Trust Bank Charter

Coinbase Joins Circle, Ripple With Final OCC Approval for Federal Trust Bank Charter

Coinbase has received final approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) to charter Coinbase National Trust Company, the crypto exchange said on Monday.

The OCC approved the application last Friday, according to Coinbase. The firm said the charter will let it expand its custody business, which holds digital assets on behalf of institutional clients, under a federal regulatory framework.

"Custody is foundational to our business," the company said, describing itself as the leading crypto custodian globally. The charter will "bring clear and consistent federal uniformity" to its custody operations, it added.

"Trusted custody is essential for bringing more of the financial system onchain," Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong tweeted on Monday, calling the trust company "another step for building that foundation."

Trusted custody is essential for bringing more of the financial system onchain.

Coinbase National Trust Company is another step for building that foundation. https://t.co/35K2yC3xpj

— Brian Armstrong (@brian_armstrong) November 9, 2026

Coinbase has offered regulated custody since 2018, when its Coinbase Custody Trust Company won a limited purpose trust charter from the New York Department of Financial Services. The new national trust company builds on that foundation while bringing its trust activities into a consistent federal framework, Coinbase said.

The approval comes seven months after the OCC gave Coinbase conditional approval in April, when the company said it was not becoming a commercial bank and would not take retail deposits or engage in fractional reserve banking. Coinbase first applied for the charter last year.

Coinbase joins a growing list of crypto firms with national trust charters. Circle won final approval in July for a trust bank to manage the reserves behind its USDC stablecoin, and Ripple received final approval last month for a trust bank behind its RLUSD stablecoin.

Others are still awaiting final approval. Jack Dorsey's Block has applied for a charter to custody Bitcoin in September, Kraken parent Payward filed its own application in May, and a trust company linked to Trump family-backed World Liberty Financial won conditional approval in August for a charter tied to its USD1 stablecoin, Reuters reported.

The approvals have drawn opposition. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) has argued that the OCC's crypto charter approvals, including Coinbase's, are illegal, and the Independent Community Bankers of America has sued the OCC in an effort to stop crypto firms from entering banking through what it describes as a side door.

Trump Media & Technology Group has pledged about 73% of its bitcoin to an options program in which the counterparty can reuse the coins, the company disclosed in its third-quarter 10-Q filed Monday, three weeks before holders of its $1 billion in convertible notes can demand cash.

The Truth Social parent held approximately 15,649 BTC on Sept. 30, Chief Financial Officer Phillip Juhan said on Monday’s earnings call, along with 7 million shares of BlackRock’s IBIT. Of those coins, 11,385.20 were pledged to what the company calls its bitcoin yield management program.

The filing says that program requires Trump Media to post bitcoin as collateral “that the counterparty can rehypothecate at their sole discretion.” The pledged coins carried a fair value of $951.4 million at quarter-end. The 10-Q does not name the counterparty.

Another 4,260.73 BTC, worth $356.1 million on Sept. 30, sits as collateral for the convertible notes and cannot be withdrawn or distributed until the indenture’s conditions are met.

Together, the two buckets account for about 15,646 BTC, nearly all of the stack Juhan described.

Trump Media sells and buys covered calls and puts on bitcoin, settled in bitcoin, to “generate yield on these assets and increase our principal balance of bitcoin,” the filing says. Premiums arrive in bitcoin and are “immediately rehypothecated to our digital asset manager to reinvest.”

At quarter-end it had written calls referencing 4,838.40 BTC at strikes from $68,000 to $92,000 and puts on 1,500 BTC at $75,000 to $80,000, all expiring in October.

A risk factor spells out the trade-off. The company says its yield counterparties “may not be rated” by credit agencies, that it is limited in its ability to sell or use deployed bitcoin while the arrangements are open, and that where they are unsecured “we may be unable to recover deployed bitcoin in a counterparty insolvency.”

Juhan said Trump Media bought 4,359 bitcoin during the quarter with proceeds from a partial sale of its IBIT position, part of a shift toward “third-party institutional” management of its treasury.

The bitcoin rally in the third quarter turned Trump Media profitable on paper. Net income was $409.7 million, driven by a $378.1 million gain on digital assets as bitcoin climbed to about $84,000 on Sept. 30 from about $59,000 on June 30. Adjusted EBITDA was still a loss of $12.3 million, and the company lost $234.2 million over the first nine months.

Prices have since moved against the stack. With bitcoin near $74,200 Tuesday morning, the 15,649 coins are worth about $1.16 billion, roughly $145 million less than at quarter-end.

The bigger test is the notes. Holders of the $1 billion in 0% senior secured convertibles, due May 2028, can require Trump Media to buy them back at full principal for cash on Nov. 30. General Counsel Scott Glabe said notices have gone out and holders have until near the end of the month to respond, so the company cannot yet say how much it will owe.

Interim CEO Kevin McGurn said the plan is “a mix of cash and credit” rather than new equity. “We want to preserve as much of our Bitcoin as possible to continue our yielding strategy and allow that asset to recover,” he said.

The 10-Q says the company may enter a new credit facility to refinance some or all of the notes, but adds that “there can be no assurance” it can do so on acceptable terms. Juhan put gross financial assets at $2.3 billion, including $182 million in cash, $211 million in short-term investments and $1.7 billion in bitcoin and bitcoin-related assets.

Trump Media is not the only treasury company under pressure. Strategy, the largest corporate holder, slipped below its average cost on Monday. Trump Media also faces more political scrutiny after Democrats won Congress, with party leaders vowing to target Trump family crypto ventures and incoming Senate Banking Chair Elizabeth Warren preparing her own oversight push.

Shareholders vote Dec. 14 on the company’s planned merger with fusion energy firm TAE Technologies, which management expects to close by year-end.
